6. Cold chain: Storage at 2–5°C and 90–95% relative humidity; transport in refrigerated containers.

 7. Quality Control and Traceability

Standardized production requires a robust quality control system:

- Good Agricultural Practices (GAP): Certification to ensure food safety and environmental sustainability.
- Traceability systems: Use of QR codes or RFID tags to track fruit from orchard to consumer.
- Regular auditing: Internal and external inspections to ensure compliance with standards.

 8. Conclusion and Future Perspectives

Standardized production technology is essential for the sustainable development of the litchi industry. By implementing uniform protocols for orchard establishment, water and nutrient management, canopy management, IPM, and postharvest handling, producers can achieve consistent fruit quality, higher yields, and better market access.

Future research should focus on:
- Development of precision agriculture technologies (e.g., remote sensing, IoT-based monitoring).
- Breeding of cultivars with improved stress tolerance and extended harvest windows.
- Optimization of postharvest treatments to extend shelf life.
- Strengthening extension services to promote adoption of standardized practices among smallholder farmers.

 References

Chen, H. B., Huang, X. M., & Li, J. G. (2018). Soil management and fertilization in litchi orchards. *Journal of Tropical and Subtropical Botany*, 26(3), 245–252.

FAO. (2021). *FAOSTAT database*. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

Menzel, C. M. (2002). The physiology of growth and cropping in lychee. *Acta Horticulturae*, 575, 39–46.

Stern, R. A., & Gazit, S. (2003). The reproductive biology of the lychee. *Horticultural Reviews*, 28, 393–453.

Zhang, X. Y., Wang, Y. H., & Liu, C. M. (2020). Standardized fertilization technology for litchi in South China. *Chinese Journal of Tropical Agriculture*, 40(2), 112–118.

title: 大豆高产栽培技术要点
text:
Key Technical Points for High-Yield Soybean Cultivation: A Comprehensive Review

 Abstract

Soybean (*Glycine max* L. Merr.) serves as a critical source of plant protein and edible oil worldwide. Achieving high and stable yields in soybean production requires the integrated application of multiple agronomic practices, including variety selection, seed treatment, precision sowing, balanced fertilization, water management, pest and disease control, and timely harvest. This paper systematically reviews the key technical points for high-yield soybean cultivation based on current agronomic research and field practices. The review emphasizes that high yield is not the result of any single factor but rather the synergistic effect of optimized genotype × environment × management interactions. Practical recommendations are provided for growers and agricultural technicians to improve soybean productivity under diverse production conditions.

Keywords: soybean; high-yield cultivation; agronomic techniques; fertilization; integrated management

---

 1. Introduction

Soybean is one of the most important grain and oil crops globally, providing approximately 30% of the world's edible vegetable oil and over 60% of plant protein for animal feed (FAO, 2021). With increasing global demand for protein and oil, improving soybean yield per unit area has become a major objective for agricultural researchers and producers. Unlike cereal crops, soybean has a relatively low harvest index and is highly sensitive to environmental stresses, making yield improvement more challenging.

High-yield soybean cultivation (targeting >3,750 kg/ha in many regions) depends on the comprehensive optimization of cultivation techniques throughout the growing season. These techniques include selecting appropriate high-yielding varieties, proper seed treatment, rational plant density, scientific nutrient management, precise water regulation, integrated pest management, and timely harvesting. This paper aims to summarize these key technical points and provide a practical framework for high-yield soybean production.

---

 2. Variety Selection and Seed Treatment

 2.1 Selection of High-Yielding Varieties

Variety selection is the foundation of high-yield cultivation. Growers should choose varieties that meet the following criteria:

- High yield potential and stability: Varieties with proven high yields across multiple years and locations.
- Adaptability to local conditions: Maturity group should match the local frost-free period and accumulated temperature. In China, for example, the Huang-Huai-Hai region typically uses summer soybean varieties with 100–110 days maturity, while the Northeast uses spring varieties with 120–130 days.
- Stress resistance: Resistance or tolerance to major local diseases (e.g., soybean mosaic virus, cyst nematode, root rot) and lodging resistance.
- Quality traits: High protein (>40%) or high oil (>20%) content depending on market purpose.

 2.2 Seed Treatment

Before sowing, seeds should be:

- Sun-dried for 1–2 days to break dormancy and improve germination.
- Graded to remove small, damaged, or diseased seeds, ensuring uniform seedling emergence.
- Coated or dressed with fungicides (e.g., carboxin, metalaxyl) and insecticides (e.g., imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) to control seed-borne and soil-borne pathogens and early-season pests.
- Inoculated with rhizobia in fields where soybean has not been grown for 3–5 years, to enhance biological nitrogen fixation.

---

 3. Soil Preparation and Sowing Techniques

 3.1 Land Preparation

Soybean prefers well-drained, fertile loam or sandy loam soils with pH 6.0–7.5. Key practices include:

- Deep tillage (20–25 cm) every 2–3 years to break the plow pan and improve root penetration.
- Fine seedbed preparation with no large clods, ensuring good seed-soil contact.
- Conservation tillage (no-till or reduced till) in erosion-prone areas, combined with residue retention.

 3.2 Sowing Time and Density

- Sowing time: Sow when soil temperature at 5 cm depth stabilizes above 10°C. In Northeast China, this is typically late April to early May; in the Huang-Huai-Hai region, mid-June after wheat harvest.
- Plant density: Optimal density varies with variety, fertility, and row spacing. Generally:
  - Dwarf or semi-dwarf varieties: 300,000–375,000 plants/ha.
  - Tall, lodging-resistant varieties: 225,000–300,000 plants/ha.
  - Narrow rows (30–45 cm) allow higher density than wide rows (60–70 cm).
- Sowing depth: 3–5 cm, depending on soil moisture and texture.
- Uniformity: Use precision seeders to ensure uniform depth and spacing, which is critical for uniform maturity and high yield.

---

 4. Nutrient Management

 4.1 Macro- and Micronutrients

Soybean requires balanced nutrition, with particular attention to nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and micronutrients (B, Mo, Zn, Mn).

- Nitrogen: Although soybean fixes atmospheric N through symbiosis, starter N (20–40 kg/ha) is beneficial, especially in cold or low-fertility soils. Excessive N suppresses nodulation.
- Phosphorus: Apply 60–90 kg P₂O₅/ha based on soil test. P is critical for root development, nodulation, and seed filling.
- Potassium: Apply 75–120 kg K₂O/ha. K improves stem strength, disease resistance, and seed quality.
- Sulfur: 20–30 kg S/ha may be needed in sandy or low-organic-matter soils.
- Micronutrients: Foliar spray of 0.1–0.2% ammonium molybdate at flowering, and 0.2% boric acid at pod initiation, can significantly improve pod set and seed weight.

 4.2 Fertilization Methods

- Base fertilizer: 60–70% of P and K applied before sowing, incorporated into the soil.
- Seed fertilizer: Small amount of N and P placed 3–5 cm below and beside seeds.
- Top dressing: Urea (30–50 kg/ha) at the early flowering stage (R1) if plants show N deficiency.
- Foliar spray: At R2–R4, spray 0.2% KH₂PO₄ + micronutrients to prevent premature senescence and promote seed filling.

 4.3 Biological Nitrogen Fixation

Inoculation with *Bradyrhizobium japonicum* can supply 50–75% of soybean N needs. Ensure adequate soil moisture, neutral pH, and sufficient P, K, Mo, and Co for optimal nodulation.

---

 5. Water Management

Soybean is sensitive to both drought and waterlogging. Critical water-sensitive periods are:

- Germination and seedling stage: Adequate soil moisture for uniform emergence.
- Flowering (R1–R2): Drought reduces flower number and pod set.
- Pod filling (R4–R6): Water stress causes pod abortion and reduced seed weight.

Irrigation: Apply 30–40 mm water when soil moisture drops below 65% of field capacity at critical stages. Drip irrigation or sprinkler irrigation is more efficient than furrow irrigation.

Drainage: Soybean is highly susceptible to waterlogging. Ensure field drainage ditches are functional, especially in low-lying areas. Waterlogging for >3 days at flowering can reduce yield by 20–40%.

---

 6. Weed, Pest, and Disease Management

 6.1 Weed Control

- Pre-emergence: Apply pendimethalin or metolachlor before emergence.
- Post-emergence: Apply quizalofop-p-ethyl or bentazone at 2–4 leaf stage of weeds.
- Mechanical: Inter-row cultivation at V2–V3 and again at V5–V6.
- Integrated: Combine chemical, mechanical, and manual methods to reduce herbicide resistance.

 6.2 Major Pests

- Aphids: Control with imidacloprid or thiamethoxam when >50% plants infested.
- Pod borers (*Helicoverpa armigera*): Use Bacillus thuringiensis or chlorantraniliprole at flowering.
- Spider mites: Spray abamectin or bifenazate during dry periods.
- Bean bug: Monitor with pheromone traps; apply insecticide at threshold.

 6.3 Major Diseases

- Soybean mosaic virus: Use resistant varieties and control aphid vectors.
- Root rot (*Phytophthora* spp.): Seed treatment with metalaxyl + fungicide rotation.
- Sclerotinia stem rot: Avoid excessive density and humidity; apply carbendazim at R1–R2.
- Frogeye leaf spot: Apply azoxystrobin or difenoconazole at first symptom.

Integrated Pest Management (IPM): Combine resistant varieties, crop rotation, biological control, and judicious pesticide use to minimize environmental impact and delay resistance.

---

 7. Harvest and Post-Harvest Handling

 7.1 Timely Harvest

- Harvest when 95% of pods are brown and seeds have <15% moisture.
- Delayed harvest increases shattering losses and reduces seed quality.
- Use combine harvesters with proper reel speed and cylinder speed to minimize grain damage.

 7.2 Storage

- Dry seeds to 12–13% moisture before storage.
- Store in clean, dry, ventilated facilities.
- Protect from insects and rodents.

---

 8. Integrated High-Yield Management Model

High yield is achieved through the synergistic integration of all practices. A typical high-yield model (e.g., 4,500 kg/ha) includes:

| Practice | Recommendation |
|----------|----------------|
| Variety | High-yielding, disease-resistant, adapted maturity group |
| Seed treatment | Fungicide + insecticide + rhizobia |
| Sowing | Precision, 30–45 cm rows, 300,000–350,000 plants/ha |
| Fertilizer | 60–90 kg P₂O₅, 75–120 kg K₂O, 20–40 kg N starter, Mo/B foliar |
| Water | Irrigate at R1–R2 and R4–R6 if needed; ensure drainage |
| Pest control | IPM with economic thresholds |
| Harvest | Timely, at 95% brown pods |

---

 9. Conclusion

High-yield soybean cultivation is a systematic endeavor requiring attention to every stage of production. Variety selection, seed treatment, precision sowing, balanced fertilization, optimal water management, integrated pest and disease control, and timely harvest are all essential components. The key to success lies in adapting these general principles to local soil, climate, and market conditions through adaptive research and farmer training. Future advances in precision agriculture, remote sensing, and decision-support systems will further enhance soybean yield potential and sustainability.

---

 References

1. FAO. (2021). *FAO Statistical Yearbook 2021*. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Rome.
2. Liu, X., et al. (2020). Integrated agronomic practices for high-yield soybean in Northeast China. *Field Crops Research*, 246, 107-118.
3. Board, J. E., & Kahlon, C. S. (2011). Soybean yield formation: What controls it and how it can be improved? *Soybean Physiology and Biochemistry*, 1–36.
4. Sinclair, T. R., & Rufty, T. W. (2012). Nitrogen and water resources commonly limit soybean yield. *Field Crops Research*, 128, 1–7.
5. Gai, J., et al. (2016). Soybean breeding and cultivation in China. *Journal of Integrative Agriculture*, 15(7), 1455–1465.
6. Pedersen, P., & Lauer, J. G. (2003). Soybean agronomic response to management systems in the Upper Midwest. *Agronomy Journal*, 95(5), 1146–1151.

---

Author Note: This paper is intended for academic and extension purposes. Growers should consult local agricultural extension services for region-specific recommendations.

title: 草莓设施栽培关键技术
text:
Here is a short academic paper on the requested topic, written in English and following the standard academic paper format.

---

 Key Technologies for Protected Cultivation of Strawberry

Author: [Author's Name]
Affiliation: [Author's Institution]
Email: [Author's Email]

---

 Abstract

Protected cultivation, encompassing greenhouse and high-tunnel systems, has revolutionized strawberry (*Fragaria* × *ananassa*) production by enabling year-round supply, extending harvest seasons, and mitigating environmental risks. This paper synthesizes the key technologies essential for successful strawberry protected cultivation. It examines critical aspects including cultivar selection, environmental control (temperature, humidity, and light), soilless substrate management, precise fertigation, and integrated pest management (IPM). The discussion highlights how the optimization and integration of these technologies are paramount for maximizing yield, improving fruit quality, and ensuring the economic sustainability of strawberry production in controlled environments.

Keywords: Strawberry, *Fragaria* × *ananassa*, Protected Cultivation, Greenhouse, Soilless Culture, Fertigation, Environmental Control

---

 1. Introduction

The strawberry is a globally significant fruit crop valued for its unique flavor, aroma, and high nutritional content. Traditionally cultivated in open fields, strawberry production is highly susceptible to climatic variations, soil-borne diseases, and pest infestations, leading to inconsistent yields and a limited harvest window. The advent of protected cultivation has fundamentally transformed the industry. By growing plants under controlled or semi-controlled environments such as greenhouses, plastic tunnels, and vertical farms, producers can overcome these limitations. This system allows for the manipulation of the growing environment to optimize plant growth, enabling off-season production, enhancing fruit quality, and significantly increasing marketable yields. The success of this system, however, hinges on the precise application of a suite of interconnected key technologies. This paper aims to outline and discuss these core technologies, providing a consolidated overview of best practices for modern strawberry protected cultivation.

 2. Core Technologies in Protected Cultivation

2.1. Cultivar Selection

The choice of cultivar is the foundational decision for any protected cultivation system. The selected cultivar must be adapted to the specific goals of the production system (e.g., winter production, summer production) and the local market. Key criteria include:

- Photoperiodic Response: The selection of short-day, long-day, or day-neutral cultivars is critical. Day-neutral cultivars are often preferred for year-round production in controlled environments as their flowering is less dependent on day length.
- Chilling Requirement: For winter production in temperate climates, cultivars with low chilling requirements are essential to ensure proper bud break and flowering.
- Disease Resistance: Selecting cultivars with genetic resistance to common diseases like powdery mildew, angular leaf spot, and *Phytophthora* crown rot is a primary strategy for reducing chemical inputs.
- Fruit Quality and Yield: High yield potential, large fruit size, firmness (for transport), and excellent flavor are crucial commercial attributes.

2.2. Environmental Control

Maintaining an optimal microclimate within the protected structure is crucial for maximizing photosynthetic efficiency and preventing physiological disorders.

- Temperature: Optimal temperatures for strawberry growth range from 18-22°C during the day and 10-13°C at night. Extreme temperatures can lead to poor pollination, fruit malformation, and reduced yield. Heating and ventilation systems are employed to maintain these ranges.
- Humidity: High relative humidity (above 80%) promotes the development of fungal diseases, particularly botrytis fruit rot. Conversely, low humidity can lead to water stress. Ventilation and dehumidification systems are used to manage humidity levels, ideally between 60-75%.
- Light: Light is the primary driver of photosynthesis. In low-light conditions (e.g., winter greenhouses), supplemental lighting using LED or HPS lamps is often necessary to maintain adequate Daily Light Integral (DLI) levels, promoting growth and flowering.
- CO₂ Enrichment: Supplementing the greenhouse atmosphere with carbon dioxide (CO₂) to levels of 800-1000 ppm can significantly enhance photosynthetic rates and increase yield.

2.3. Soilless Culture and Substrate Management

Soilless culture has become a standard practice in protected strawberry production, offering numerous advantages over traditional soil-based systems. It eliminates soil-borne pathogens, allows for precise control over water and nutrient delivery, and facilitates vertical farming.

- Growing Systems: Common systems include raised troughs, grow bags, and vertical towers filled with a sterile substrate.
- Substrates: The ideal substrate must have high water-holding capacity, good aeration, and be chemically inert. Common materials include a mix of coco coir, peat moss, perlite, and rockwool. Coco coir is particularly popular due to its excellent water retention and aeration properties.
- Sterilization: To prevent disease recurrence, substrates are often sterilized between crop cycles using steam, solarization, or chemical fumigants.

2.4. Fertigation and Nutrient Management

Fertigation, the injection of fertilizers into the irrigation water, is a cornerstone of soilless culture. It allows for the precise and timely delivery of essential nutrients directly to the root zone.

- Nutrient Solution: A balanced nutrient solution containing all macro- and microelements is essential. The composition is typically adjusted based on the plant's growth stage (vegetative vs. reproductive) and environmental conditions.
- EC and pH Monitoring: The Electrical Conductivity (EC) of the nutrient solution, which indicates its total salt concentration, and the pH, which affects nutrient availability, must be monitored and maintained within optimal ranges (e.g., EC: 1.0-1.5 dS/m, pH: 5.8-6.2).
- Irrigation Scheduling: The frequency and duration of irrigation events are critical. Over-irrigation can lead to root hypoxia and nutrient leaching, while under-irrigation causes water stress. Scheduling is often based on solar radiation, substrate moisture sensors, or a fixed timer.

2.5. Integrated Pest and Disease Management (IPM)

The warm, humid, and dense environment of a protected structure is conducive to pest and disease outbreaks. An IPM strategy is vital for sustainable production.

- Preventive Measures: This includes starting with certified disease-free transplants, maintaining strict sanitation protocols (e.g., disinfecting tools, removing plant debris), and managing environmental conditions to discourage pathogens.
- Biological Control: The use of natural enemies, such as predatory mites (*Phytoseiulus persimilis*) for spider mites and parasitic wasps (*Encarsia formosa*) for whiteflies, is a key component of IPM.
- Monitoring and Thresholds: Regular scouting and the use of sticky traps are necessary to monitor pest populations. Chemical pesticides are used only as a last resort when pest populations exceed established action thresholds, and selecting products with low toxicity to beneficial insects is prioritized.

 3. Conclusion

The successful protected cultivation of strawberries is a sophisticated agricultural practice that relies on the seamless integration of multiple key technologies. From the strategic selection of a suitable cultivar and the precise control of the microclimate to the implementation of a robust soilless fertigation system and a proactive IPM program, each component is critical. The future of the industry lies in further automation, the use of sensor-based decision support systems, and the development of more energy-efficient and sustainable growing systems. By mastering these technologies, growers can continue to meet the global demand for high-quality strawberries, ensuring production stability and economic viability in an ever-changing world.

---

 References

[1] Hancock, J. F. (1999). *Strawberries*. CABI Publishing.
[2] Lieten, F. (2005). Protected cultivation of strawberries: a review. *Acta Horticulturae*, (708), 37-44.
[3] Sonsteby, A., & Heide, O. M. (2007). Long-day control of flowering in everbearing strawberries. *Journal of Horticultural Science and Biotechnology*, 82(6), 875-884.
[4] Trejo-Téllez, L. I., & Gómez-Merino, F. C. (2012). Nutrient management in strawberry: effects on yield, quality and plant health. In *Strawberries: Cultivation, Antioxidant Properties and Health Benefits* (pp. 1-36). Nova Science Publishers.
[5] Van Lenteren, J. C. (2012). The state of commercial augmentative biological control: plenty of natural enemies, but a frustrating lack of uptake. *BioControl*, 57(1), 1-20.

title: 葱产业发展现状与对策
text:
Current Status and Countermeasures of the Green Onion Industry: A Short Review

 Abstract

The green onion (*Allium fistulosum* L.) is an economically important vegetable crop widely cultivated in East Asia and other regions. This paper briefly reviews the current status of the green onion industry, including production distribution, market demand, and industrial chain development, and identifies major challenges such as low mechanization, postharvest losses, price volatility, and weak brand building. Corresponding countermeasures are proposed, including breeding improvement, mechanized production, cold-chain logistics, deep processing, and brand marketing, in order to provide references for the sustainable and high-quality development of the green onion industry.

Keywords: green onion; industry status; problems; countermeasures; sustainable development

 1. Introduction

The green onion, also known as Welsh onion or bunching onion, is a widely consumed condiment and vegetable crop. It is rich in volatile oils, vitamins, and minerals, and plays an important role in daily diets and food processing. In recent years, with the adjustment of agricultural structure and the growth of market demand, the green onion industry has expanded rapidly in planting area and output. However, the industry still faces multiple constraints in production, processing, and marketing. This paper aims to summarize the current situation and propose feasible countermeasures.

 2. Current Status of the Green Onion Industry

 2.1 Production Scale and Distribution

Green onion is mainly produced in China, Japan, South Korea, and Southeast Asian countries. China is the largest producer and exporter. Major production areas in China include Shandong, Hebei, Henan, Liaoning, and Yunnan provinces. Production is characterized by regional concentration and seasonal complementarity, which ensures year-round supply to a certain extent.

 2.2 Market Demand

Demand for green onion comes from household consumption, catering services, and food processing. With urbanization and the development of the catering industry, demand has remained stable and even increased. Meanwhile, export demand, especially from Japan, South Korea, and Southeast Asia, has promoted the development of standardized production bases.

 2.3 Industrial Chain Development

The industrial chain mainly includes breeding, cultivation, harvesting, primary processing (cleaning, sorting, packaging), storage and transportation, and sales. In recent years, some leading enterprises and cooperatives have begun to establish integrated operations covering production, processing, and marketing, but the overall level of industrialization remains uneven.

 3. Major Problems

 3.1 Weak Breeding and Seed Supply System

Most varieties are traditional local varieties, and the breeding of varieties with strong stress resistance, high yield, and good quality lags behind. Seed quality is uneven, which affects yield and product consistency.

 3.2 Low Level of Mechanization

Green onion production, especially transplanting and harvesting, relies heavily on manual labor. Labor intensity is high, and labor costs continue to rise, reducing farmers' profits and restricting large-scale production.

 3.3 Postharvest Losses and Weak Cold-Chain Logistics

Green onion is perishable and sensitive to temperature and humidity. In many areas, harvesting, precooling, storage, and transportation facilities are insufficient, resulting in high postharvest loss and short shelf life.

 3.4 Price Volatility and Market Risk

Due to small-scale production and information asymmetry, prices fluctuate sharply. Farmers often make planting decisions based on previous prices, leading to periodic oversupply or shortage.

 3.5 Insufficient Deep Processing and Brand Building

Most green onion is sold as fresh products. Deep processing products such as dried onion, frozen onion, onion oil, and seasoning products are limited. Regional brands are few, and market competitiveness is weak.

 4. Countermeasures and Suggestions

 4.1 Strengthening Breeding and Seed Industry

It is necessary to increase investment in breeding programs, develop excellent varieties adapted to different ecological regions, and promote certified seed production and standardized seed management. Cooperation among research institutes, universities, and enterprises should be encouraged.

 4.2 Promoting Mechanized and Standardized Production

Research and development of specialized machinery for transplanting, fertilization, and harvesting should be accelerated. Standardized cultivation techniques, including reasonable density, water and fertilizer management, and pest control, should be promoted to improve yield and quality.

 4.3 Improving Postharvest and Cold-Chain Systems

Precooling, cleaning, grading, and packaging facilities should be established near production areas. Cold-chain logistics should be improved to extend shelf life and reduce losses. Government support for cold-storage infrastructure is essential.

 4.4 Developing Deep Processing and Diversified Products

Enterprises should be encouraged to develop deep-processed products such as dehydrated green onion, frozen products, and functional seasonings. This can increase added value, stabilize demand, and reduce reliance on the fresh market.

 4.5 Strengthening Market Information and Risk Management

An information service platform should be built to release planting, price, and demand information in a timely manner. Farmers' cooperatives and industry associations should play a greater role in guiding production and coordinating sales. Agricultural insurance and futures tools can also help mitigate price risks.

 4.6 Building Brands and Expanding Markets

Regional public brands should be cultivated based on local advantages. Quality certification and traceability systems should be established. E-commerce and export channels should be expanded to enhance brand influence and international competitiveness.

 5. Conclusion

The green onion industry has a broad market prospect, but its development is constrained by weak breeding, low mechanization, postharvest losses, price fluctuations, and insufficient processing and branding. By strengthening scientific and technological support, improving the industrial chain, and enhancing market regulation, the industry can move toward scale, standardization, and sustainability. Coordinated efforts from government, enterprises, cooperatives, and farmers are required to achieve high-quality development of the green onion industry.

 References

[1] Zhang, Y., & Li, H. (2020). Current situation and development countermeasures of green onion industry in China. *Journal of Vegetable Science*, 32(4), 45–50.

[2] Wang, L., & Chen, X. (2019). Research on mechanized production technology of bunching onion. *Agricultural Engineering and Technology*, 39(6), 22–26.

[3] Liu, J., & Zhao, M. (2021). Postharvest preservation and cold-chain logistics of leafy vegetables. *Food Science and Technology*, 46(3), 112–118.

[4] Kim, S., & Park, J. (2018). Production and marketing of Welsh onion in East Asia. *Horticulture, Environment, and Biotechnology*, 59(2), 201–210.

title: 生姜养殖技术与效益分析
text:
Ginger Cultivation Techniques and Benefit Analysis: A Comprehensive Study

 Abstract

Ginger (Zingiber officinale Roscoe) is an important economic crop widely cultivated in tropical and subtropical regions. This paper systematically reviews the key cultivation techniques for ginger, including site selection, seed preparation, planting methods, field management, and pest control. Furthermore, it analyzes the economic benefits of ginger production from multiple perspectives, including yield, cost structure, market pricing, and profitability. The study aims to provide theoretical guidance and practical references for ginger growers and agricultural practitioners seeking to optimize production and maximize returns.

Keywords: ginger; cultivation techniques; benefit analysis; economic returns; field management

---

 1. Introduction

Ginger is a perennial herbaceous plant belonging to the family Zingiberaceae. It is widely used as a spice, culinary ingredient, and traditional medicine across the globe. Global ginger production has steadily increased over the past decades, driven by rising demand in both food and pharmaceutical industries. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the world's total ginger production exceeded 4 million metric tons in recent years, with China and India being the largest producers.

Despite its economic importance, many ginger farmers face challenges such as low yields, disease outbreaks, and market price fluctuations. Therefore, understanding proper cultivation techniques and conducting thorough benefit analysis are essential for sustainable ginger production. This paper addresses these issues by examining the complete production cycle and evaluating the economic viability of ginger farming.

---

 2. Botanical Characteristics and Environmental Requirements

 2.1 Botanical Description

Ginger is a rhizomatous herb that grows to a height of 0.5–1.5 meters. The underground rhizome, which is the commercially valuable part, is thick, fleshy, and aromatic. Leaves are lanceolate, arranged alternately, and the flowers are rarely produced under cultivation.

 2.2 Climate Requirements

Ginger thrives in warm and humid climates with temperatures ranging from 20°C to 30°C. It requires a frost-free growing period of 8–10 months. Optimal rainfall ranges between 1,500 and 2,500 mm per year. Excessive heat above 35°C or prolonged drought can significantly reduce yield.

 2.3 Soil Requirements

Well-drained sandy loam or loamy soils with a pH of 5.5–6.5 are ideal for ginger cultivation. The soil should be rich in organic matter and free from waterlogging, as ginger rhizomes are highly susceptible to rot in saturated conditions.

---

 3. Cultivation Techniques

 3.1 Site Selection and Land Preparation

Selecting an appropriate site is the first critical step. The field should have good drainage, adequate sunlight, and a history free from ginger diseases. Land preparation involves deep plowing to a depth of 30–40 cm, followed by harrowing to break clods. Raised beds of 1–1.2 m width and 15–25 cm height are recommended to improve drainage.

 3.2 Seed Rhizome Selection and Treatment

High-quality seed rhizomes are essential for vigorous growth. Healthy rhizomes weighing 20–30 g with at least one or two well-developed buds should be selected. Before planting, seed rhizomes are typically treated with fungicides (e.g., carbendazim) and sometimes dipped in biofertilizer solutions to enhance sprouting and disease resistance.

 3.3 Planting

Planting is usually done at the beginning of the rainy season. Seed rhizomes are planted at a spacing of 25–30 cm between plants and 30–40 cm between rows, at a depth of 5–8 cm. The seed rate varies between 1,500 and 2,500 kg per hectare, depending on the variety and spacing.

 3.4 Fertilization

Ginger is a heavy feeder and responds well to organic and inorganic fertilizers. A typical fertilization program includes:

- Basal application: Farmyard manure (20–30 t/ha), phosphorus (50–60 kg P₂O₅/ha), and potassium (50–60 kg K₂O/ha).
- Top dressing: Nitrogen (60–80 kg N/ha) applied in two or three split doses during the growing season.
- Micronutrients: Zinc and boron may be applied if deficiency symptoms appear.

 3.5 Irrigation and Water Management

Consistent soil moisture is crucial for ginger growth. Irrigation should be provided during dry spells, but waterlogging must be avoided. Drip irrigation combined with mulching is an efficient method to conserve water and suppress weeds.

 3.6 Mulching

Mulching with organic materials such as straw, dry leaves, or plastic film helps conserve moisture, regulate soil temperature, and reduce weed competition. It also promotes rhizome development by maintaining a favorable soil environment.

 3.7 Weed Control

Weeds compete with ginger for nutrients, water, and light. Manual weeding is commonly practiced, especially during the early growth stages. Herbicides such as glyphosate may be used pre-planting, but care must be taken to avoid crop injury.

 3.8 Pest and Disease Management

Major diseases of ginger include:

- Rhizome rot (Pythium spp.): Managed through seed treatment, crop rotation, and improved drainage.
- Bacterial wilt (Ralstonia solanacearum): Controlled by using resistant varieties and avoiding infected fields.
- Leaf spot (Phyllosticta zingiberi): Treated with fungicidal sprays.

Common pests include shoot borers, aphids, and root-knot nematodes. Integrated Pest Management (IPM) strategies combining cultural, biological, and chemical methods are recommended.

 3.9 Harvesting

Ginger is typically harvested 8–10 months after planting. Fresh ginger is harvested when rhizomes are tender, while mature ginger for drying is harvested when leaves turn yellow and begin to dry. Harvesting involves carefully lifting the rhizomes with a spade or fork to avoid damage.

 3.10 Post-Harvest Handling

After harvesting, rhizomes are washed, graded, and either sold fresh or processed (dried, pickled, or powdered). Proper curing and storage at 10–15°C with 85–90% relative humidity extend shelf life.

---

 4. Benefit Analysis

 4.1 Yield Performance

Under optimal management, ginger yields range from 15 to 30 t/ha for fresh rhizomes. High-input systems with improved varieties and drip irrigation can achieve up to 40 t/ha. Dry ginger yield is approximately 20–25% of fresh weight.

 4.2 Cost Structure

Major cost components per hectare include:

| Cost Item | Approximate Cost (USD/ha) |
|---|---|
| Seed rhizomes | 3,000–5,000 |
| Land preparation | 500–800 |
| Fertilizers | 800–1,200 |
| Pesticides | 300–600 |
| Labor | 2,000–3,500 |
| Irrigation | 400–700 |
| Mulching materials | 300–500 |
| Miscellaneous | 300–500 |
| Total | 7,600–12,800 |

 4.3 Revenue and Profitability

Assuming an average yield of 20 t/ha and a market price of USD 0.80–1.50 per kg for fresh ginger, gross revenue ranges from USD 16,000 to 30,000 per hectare. Net profit, after deducting total costs, ranges from USD 8,000 to 17,000 per hectare. The benefit-cost ratio typically ranges from 1.8 to 2.5, indicating favorable economic returns.

 4.4 Value Addition

Processing ginger into dried ginger, ginger powder, ginger oil, or ginger oleoresin can significantly increase profit margins. For example, dried ginger fetches 3–5 times the price of fresh ginger in international markets. Small-scale processing units can add substantial value at the farm level.

 4.5 Market Considerations

Ginger prices are subject to seasonal fluctuations and global market dynamics. Farmers can mitigate price risks through contract farming, cooperative marketing, and diversification into processed products. Organic certification also offers premium prices in developed markets.

---

 5. Challenges and Recommendations

 5.1 Challenges

- High incidence of soil-borne diseases
- Volatile market prices
- High initial investment
- Limited access to quality planting materials
- Climate change impacts

 5.2 Recommendations

1. Adopt integrated disease management practices.
2. Use certified disease-free seed rhizomes.
3. Implement drip irrigation and mulching for water efficiency.
4. Diversify into value-added products.
5. Strengthen farmer cooperatives for better market access.
6. Invest in research and extension services.

---

 6. Conclusion

Ginger cultivation offers significant economic potential when proper techniques are applied. Key success factors include careful site selection, use of quality seed rhizomes, balanced fertilization, effective pest and disease management, and timely harvesting. The benefit analysis indicates that ginger farming can yield net profits of USD 8,000–17,000 per hectare with a benefit-cost ratio of 1.8–2.5. Value addition and market diversification further enhance profitability. With growing global demand for ginger and its derivatives, sustainable and scientific cultivation practices will be essential for maximizing both productivity and economic returns.

---

 References

1. Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO). (2022). *FAOSTAT Database*. Rome: FAO.
2. Ravindran, P. N., & Babu, K. N. (2005). *Ginger: The Genus Zingiber*. CRC Press.
3. Nybe, E. V., & Peter, K. V. (2007). *Spices*. New India Publishing Agency.
4. Sharma, R. K., & Singh, B. (2019). "Integrated Disease Management in Ginger." *Journal of Spices and Aromatic Crops*, 28(1), 12–22.
5. Kizhakkayil, J., & Sasikumar, B. (2011). "Diversity, Characterization and Utilization of Ginger." *Plant Genetic Resources*, 9(3), 431–439.

---

*This paper is intended for academic and practical reference purposes. Actual costs, yields, and prices may vary depending on region, variety, and market conditions.*

title: 白菜高产栽培技术要点
text:
Key Techniques for High-Yield Cultivation of Chinese Cabbage: A Comprehensive Review

 Abstract

Chinese cabbage (*Brassica rapa* subsp. *pekinensis*) is one of the most economically important leafy vegetables in East Asia, particularly in China, Korea, and Japan. Achieving high yield and superior quality in Chinese cabbage production requires an integrated approach encompassing cultivar selection, soil preparation, precision sowing, water and nutrient management, pest and disease control, and timely harvest. This paper systematically reviews the key agronomic practices that contribute to high-yield cultivation of Chinese cabbage. The review emphasizes the importance of site-specific management strategies, balanced fertilization based on soil testing, optimized planting density, drip irrigation and fertigation, and integrated pest management (IPM). The findings provide a practical framework for growers and researchers aiming to enhance productivity and sustainability in Chinese cabbage production systems.

Keywords: Chinese cabbage; high-yield cultivation; fertilization; planting density; water management; integrated pest management; *Brassica rapa*

 1. Introduction

Chinese cabbage (*Brassica rapa* subsp. *pekinensis*), also known as napa cabbage or Peking cabbage, is a cool-season biennial vegetable belonging to the Brassicaceae family. It is widely cultivated across East Asia and has gained increasing popularity in other regions due to its adaptability, nutritional value, and culinary versatility. China alone accounts for over 70% of global Chinese cabbage production, with annual output exceeding 100 million tons (FAO, 2022).

Despite its economic significance, Chinese cabbage production faces numerous challenges, including climate variability, soil degradation, pest and disease outbreaks, and inefficient resource utilization. These challenges necessitate the development and adoption of science-based cultivation techniques to achieve high yields while maintaining environmental sustainability.

High-yield cultivation of Chinese cabbage is not achieved through a single factor but rather through the synergistic optimization of multiple agronomic practices. This paper aims to synthesize current knowledge on key cultivation techniques, including cultivar selection, soil and seedbed preparation, sowing and transplanting, water and fertilizer management, pest and disease control, and harvest timing. The objective is to provide a comprehensive reference for researchers, extension agents, and commercial growers.

 2. Key Cultivation Techniques

 2.1 Cultivar Selection

The choice of cultivar is the foundational step in high-yield Chinese cabbage production. Cultivars should be selected based on local climatic conditions, market preferences, and resistance to prevalent diseases. Key criteria include:

- Adaptability: Cultivars must be adapted to the local photoperiod and temperature regime. Chinese cabbage is sensitive to bolting, which is triggered by low temperatures and long-day conditions. Therefore, bolting-resistant cultivars are essential for spring and early summer planting.
- Disease resistance: Resistance to major diseases such as soft rot (*Erwinia carotovora*), downy mildew (*Peronospora parasitica*), and turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) significantly reduces yield losses.
- Yield potential and quality: High-yielding cultivars with compact heads, good internal quality (e.g., high soluble solids, tender texture), and desirable head weight (typically 2–4 kg) are preferred.

In China, widely planted cultivars include 'Beijing New No. 3', 'Zhongbai No. 78', and 'Jinza No. 60', which exhibit strong resistance to TuMV and downy mildew (Zhang et al., 2019).

 2.2 Soil and Seedbed Preparation

Chinese cabbage thrives in well-drained, fertile soils with a pH of 6.0–7.5. Loamy or sandy loam soils with high organic matter content are ideal. Proper soil preparation is critical for root development and nutrient uptake.

- Deep plowing: Plowing to a depth of 25–30 cm improves soil aeration and root penetration.
- Organic amendment: Application of well-decomposed farmyard manure (30–45 t/ha) or compost improves soil structure, water-holding capacity, and microbial activity.
- Raised beds: In regions with heavy rainfall or poor drainage, raised beds (15–20 cm high) are recommended to prevent waterlogging and reduce the incidence of soft rot.
- Soil testing: Pre-planting soil tests should be conducted to determine baseline nutrient levels and guide fertilization programs.

 2.3 Sowing and Transplanting

Optimal sowing time and planting density are crucial for maximizing yield.

- Sowing time: Chinese cabbage is typically grown in autumn in most regions of China, with sowing from late July to mid-August. Spring cultivation is possible with bolting-resistant cultivars, sown from late March to early April. Soil temperature should be above 10°C for germination.
- Direct sowing vs. transplanting: Direct sowing reduces transplanting shock and labor costs, but transplanting allows for better stand establishment and uniform spacing. Transplanting is recommended for spring crops to ensure uniform maturity.
- Planting density: Optimal density varies with cultivar and season. Generally, 30,000–45,000 plants/ha are recommended, with spacing of 40–50 cm between rows and 30–40 cm between plants. Higher densities may increase total yield but reduce individual head weight and increase disease pressure (Li et al., 2020).

 2.4 Water Management

Chinese cabbage has a shallow root system and requires consistent soil moisture throughout the growing season. Water stress can lead to poor head formation, while excessive moisture promotes soft rot and other diseases.

- Irrigation scheduling: Soil moisture should be maintained at 60–80% of field capacity. Drip irrigation is preferred over furrow irrigation for its water-use efficiency and ability to deliver nutrients directly to the root zone.
- Critical periods: The most critical periods for water supply are the rosette stage and head formation stage. Water shortage during head formation can severely reduce yield and quality.
- Drainage: Excess water must be drained promptly, especially during rainy seasons, to prevent waterlogging and disease outbreaks.

 2.5 Fertilization Management

Balanced fertilization based on soil testing and crop demand is essential for high yield. Chinese cabbage has a high demand for nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K), with a typical N:P₂O₅:K₂O ratio of 1:0.4:1.2.

- Basal fertilizer: Apply 40–50% of total N, all P, and 30–40% of K as basal fertilizer before planting. Organic manure should be incorporated into the soil.
- Top dressing: Apply the remaining N and K in two or three split applications: at the rosette stage, early head formation, and mid-head formation. Avoid excessive N application, which can lead to nitrate accumulation and increased susceptibility to soft rot.
- Micronutrients: Boron and calcium are critical for head development. Boron deficiency can cause hollow stem and heart rot. Foliar sprays of 0.2% borax and 0.5% calcium chloride at the rosette and head formation stages can prevent these disorders.
- Fertigation: Integration of fertilization with drip irrigation (fertigation) improves nutrient use efficiency and reduces leaching losses (Wang et al., 2021).

 2.6 Pest and Disease Management

Integrated pest management (IPM) combines cultural, biological, and chemical control methods to minimize yield losses while reducing environmental impact.

Major diseases:
- Soft rot (*Erwinia carotovora*): Controlled through crop rotation, raised beds, avoiding overhead irrigation, and timely harvest. Chemical control is limited; copper-based bactericides may provide partial protection.
- Downy mildew (*Peronospora parasitica*): Managed with resistant cultivars, proper spacing for air circulation, and fungicide applications (e.g., metalaxyl, mancozeb) when weather conditions favor disease development.
- Turnip mosaic virus (TuMV): Transmitted by aphids. Control relies on resistant cultivars, aphid management, and removal of infected plants.
- Clubroot (*Plasmodiophora brassicae*): Managed through soil liming (pH > 7.0), crop rotation with non-brassica crops, and resistant cultivars.

Major pests:
- Aphids: Vectors of TuMV. Controlled with reflective mulches, biological control (lady beetles, parasitic wasps), and targeted insecticide applications.
- Diamondback moth (*Plutella xylostella*): Managed with *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt) formulations, pheromone traps, and judicious use of insecticides.
- Cabbage worm (*Pieris rapae*): Controlled with Bt, handpicking, and insecticides as needed.

 2.7 Harvest and Postharvest Handling

Timely harvest is critical for maximizing yield and quality. Chinese cabbage should be harvested when heads are firm and fully developed but before over-maturity, which leads to splitting and reduced storability.

- Harvest timing: Autumn crops are typically harvested 70–90 days after sowing, depending on cultivar and growing conditions. Spring crops mature in 60–75 days.
- Harvest method: Cut the stem at the base, remove outer damaged leaves, and handle carefully to avoid bruising.
- Postharvest storage: Chinese cabbage can be stored at 0–2°C and 90–95% relative humidity for 2–3 months. Proper curing and ventilation during storage reduce postharvest losses.

 3. Conclusion

High-yield cultivation of Chinese cabbage requires an integrated and site-specific approach that combines careful cultivar selection, optimal soil and water management, balanced fertilization, and robust pest and disease control. Key practices include:

1. Selecting bolting-resistant, disease-resistant, high-yielding cultivars adapted to local conditions.
2. Preparing well-drained, fertile soil with adequate organic matter and proper bed formation.
3. Optimizing planting density and sowing time to balance yield and quality.
4. Implementing drip irrigation and fertigation to improve water and nutrient use efficiency.
5. Applying balanced fertilization with split applications of N and K, and supplementing with B and Ca.
6. Adopting IPM strategies to minimize pest and disease damage while reducing chemical inputs.
7. Harvesting at optimal maturity and ensuring proper postharvest handling.

Future research should focus on precision agriculture technologies, climate-resilient cultivars, and sustainable intensification practices to further enhance Chinese cabbage productivity and sustainability.

 References

1. FAO. (2022). *FAOSTAT Database*. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Rome.

2. Li, X., Wang, Y., & Zhang, H. (2020). Effects of planting density on yield and quality of Chinese cabbage. *Journal of Horticultural Science and Biotechnology*, 95(4), 512–520.

3. Wang, J., Liu, Q., & Chen, L. (2021). Fertigation improves nutrient use efficiency and yield of Chinese cabbage in greenhouse production. *Agricultural Water Management*, 245, 106–115.

4. Zhang, S., Li, M., & Zhao, Y. (2019). Breeding of Chinese cabbage for disease resistance and high yield in China. *Acta Horticulturae*, 1256, 45–52.

5. Chen, W., & Yang, L. (2018). Integrated pest management in Chinese cabbage production: A review. *Crop Protection*, 110, 1–10.

6. Liu, Y., & Sun, X. (2020). Soil management and fertilization strategies for sustainable Chinese cabbage production. *Soil and Tillage Research*, 198, 104–112.

7. Kim, J., & Lee, S. (2017). Postharvest handling and storage of Chinese cabbage. *Postharvest Biology and Technology*, 130, 45–53.

8. Zhao, H., & Wu, P. (2021). Water requirements and irrigation scheduling for Chinese cabbage: A review. *Irrigation Science*, 39(2), 215–226.

9. Yang, R., & Huang, J. (2019). Micronutrient management in Chinese cabbage: Boron and calcium. *Journal of Plant Nutrition*, 42(8), 923–935.

10. Xu, L., & Zhou, M. (2022). Climate change impacts on Chinese cabbage production and adaptation strategies. *Climatic Change*, 170(3), 45–62.

title: 葡萄品质提升与增效途径
text:
Approaches to Improving Grape Quality and Production Efficiency: A Review

Abstract

Grape (*Vitis vinifera* L.) is one of the most economically important fruit crops worldwide. With increasing consumer demand for high-quality fruit and the need for sustainable production, improving grape quality and enhancing production efficiency have become central objectives in viticulture research. This paper reviews current approaches to grape quality improvement and efficiency enhancement, including genetic improvement and breeding, canopy and vineyard management, water and nutrient regulation, plant growth regulator application, postharvest handling, and precision agriculture technologies. The integration of these strategies is discussed, and future directions are proposed. It is concluded that a multidisciplinary, site-specific approach combining genetic, agronomic, and technological tools is essential for achieving simultaneous gains in grape quality and production efficiency.

Keywords: grape; quality improvement; production efficiency; viticulture; precision agriculture

---

 1. Introduction

Grape (*Vitis vinifera* L.) is cultivated on approximately 7.3 million hectares globally, with an annual production exceeding 70 million tonnes (OIV, 2023). Grapes are consumed fresh, dried, or processed into juice, wine, and other products, contributing substantially to agricultural economies in both temperate and subtropical regions. In recent decades, the focus of viticulture has shifted from maximizing yield to optimizing quality, driven by consumer preferences, premium market incentives, and the need for sustainable resource use.

Grape quality is a complex trait encompassing berry size, color, soluble solids content (SSC), titratable acidity (TA), phenolic compounds, aroma volatiles, and texture. Production efficiency, on the other hand, refers to the output of quality fruit per unit of input (land, water, labor, nutrients, and energy). These two objectives are not inherently contradictory; with appropriate management, quality and efficiency can be improved simultaneously.

This paper aims to review the major approaches to improving grape quality and production efficiency, synthesize current knowledge, and identify future research directions.

 2. Genetic Improvement and Breeding

Genetic improvement provides the foundation for long-term gains in both quality and efficiency. Traditional breeding has produced numerous cultivars with improved fruit characteristics, disease resistance, and environmental adaptation. However, the long generation cycle of grapevines (3–5 years to first fruiting) limits the pace of conventional breeding.

Marker-assisted selection (MAS) has accelerated the introgression of major genes, such as those controlling seedlessness, berry color, and aroma profiles. More recently, genomic selection (GS) has enabled the prediction of complex traits—including SSC, acidity, and phenolic content—using genome-wide markers, thereby shortening breeding cycles and increasing selection accuracy (Viana et al., 2020).

Emerging biotechnologies, including gene editing via CRISPR/Cas9, offer precise modification of quality-related genes. For example, editing of *VvMYBA1* and *VvMYBA2* has been shown to alter anthocyanin accumulation, potentially improving berry color and antioxidant capacity. Nevertheless, regulatory frameworks and consumer acceptance remain significant considerations for the commercialization of edited grapevines.

 3. Canopy and Vineyard Management

Canopy architecture directly influences light interception, air circulation, and microclimate within the fruit zone, all of which affect berry composition. Practices such as shoot positioning, leaf removal, shoot thinning, and cluster thinning are widely used to manipulate the leaf-to-fruit ratio and improve fruit exposure.

Basal leaf removal around the cluster zone, particularly at pre-bloom or veraison, has been consistently reported to increase berry phenolic content, reduce bunch rot incidence, and improve color uniformity (Poni et al., 2018). However, excessive leaf removal may reduce photosynthetic capacity and lead to sunburn damage, highlighting the need for site-specific optimization.

Training systems also play a critical role. Vertical shoot positioning (VSP) is common in cool-climate regions for its favorable light distribution, while divided canopy systems such as Scott Henry or Geneva Double Curtain are used in vigorous vineyards to balance vegetative growth and fruit quality. The choice of training system should consider cultivar vigor, row spacing, and mechanization potential.

 4. Water and Nutrient Regulation

Water availability is a major determinant of berry size, composition, and yield. Regulated deficit irrigation (RDI) and partial root-zone drying (PRD) have emerged as effective strategies to control vegetative growth, enhance water use efficiency (WUE), and improve fruit quality. Moderate water stress during veraison to harvest typically increases the concentration of sugars, anthocyanins, and flavor compounds while reducing yield only marginally, thereby improving the quality-to-input ratio (Chaves et al., 2010).

Nutrient management, particularly of nitrogen (N), potassium (K), and calcium (Ca), is equally important. Excessive N promotes vegetative vigor at the expense of fruit quality and increases susceptibility to pests and diseases. Precision fertilization based on soil and petiole analysis, combined with fertigation, allows for site-specific nutrient supply, reducing leaching losses and improving nutrient use efficiency.

Organic amendments and cover cropping contribute to soil health, microbial diversity, and long-term vineyard sustainability. Leguminous cover crops can fix atmospheric nitrogen, while grass covers compete with vines for water and nutrients, offering a tool for vigor control in high-fertility soils.

 5. Plant Growth Regulators

Plant growth regulators (PGRs) are widely used to manipulate grape development and improve quality. Gibberellic acid (GA₃) is applied to induce seedlessness and elongate clusters in table grapes. Forchlorfenuron (CPPU) and thidiazuron (TDZ) are used to increase berry size, although excessive use may reduce firmness and flavor.

Abscisic acid (ABA) and its analogs have been shown to promote anthocyanin biosynthesis and accelerate ripening, particularly in red cultivars grown in warm climates where color development is often insufficient. Ethephon is used to synchronize ripening and facilitate mechanical harvesting, thereby reducing labor costs and improving operational efficiency.

The application of PGRs must be carefully timed and dosed to avoid negative effects on berry texture, storage life, and consumer acceptance. Integrated use with cultural practices often yields more consistent results than PGR application alone.

 6. Postharvest Handling and Storage

Postharvest losses in table grapes can reach 20–30% due to dehydration, decay, and berry drop. Sulfur dioxide (SO₂) pads remain the most effective commercial treatment for controlling *Botrytis cinerea* and maintaining rachis freshness. However, residues and consumer concerns have prompted research into alternative treatments, including ozone, essential oils, chitosan coatings, and modified atmosphere packaging (MAP).

Controlled atmosphere (CA) storage with elevated CO₂ and reduced O₂ extends shelf life and preserves quality attributes. Edible coatings based on polysaccharides, proteins, or lipids can reduce water loss and gas exchange, thereby maintaining berry firmness and appearance. Cold chain management from harvest to retail is critical for minimizing quality deterioration and reducing food waste, which directly contributes to production efficiency.

 7. Precision Agriculture and Digital Technologies

Precision viticulture integrates remote sensing, proximal sensing, GPS, GIS, and decision support systems to manage spatial and temporal variability within vineyards. Multispectral and hyperspectral imagery can estimate canopy vigor, leaf area index, and berry composition non-destructively, enabling zone-specific management of irrigation, fertilization, and harvest.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellite platforms provide high-resolution data for mapping variability in soil, water status, and disease incidence. Proximal sensors mounted on tractors or harvesters can measure yield and quality parameters in real time, supporting selective harvesting and traceability.

Decision support systems (DSS) that integrate weather, soil, phenology, and market data help growers optimize management decisions. The adoption of these technologies can reduce input use, increase labor efficiency, and improve fruit consistency, thereby enhancing both quality and efficiency.

 8. Integration of Approaches

No single approach can simultaneously optimize all quality and efficiency objectives. Integrated vineyard management (IVM) combines genetic, cultural, physiological, and technological tools in a site-specific manner. For example, a premium red wine vineyard might combine a moderately vigorous rootstock, RDI, basal leaf removal, and precision harvest based on sensor-derived maturity maps. Such integration requires knowledge of cultivar-environment-management interactions and continuous monitoring.

Economic analysis is essential to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of individual and combined practices. While some technologies (e.g., UAVs, DSS) require initial investment, they often yield returns through improved quality, reduced inputs, and labor savings. Extension and training programs are critical for facilitating adoption, particularly among smallholder growers.

 9. Conclusion and Future Directions

Improving grape quality and production efficiency requires a multidisciplinary approach that integrates genetics, agronomy, physiology, postharvest science, and digital technology. Significant progress has been made in understanding the physiological basis of quality formation and in developing tools for precise management. However, challenges remain, including climate change, water scarcity, labor shortages, and evolving consumer demands.

Future research should focus on: (1) developing climate-resilient cultivars with superior quality traits; (2) optimizing deficit irrigation and nutrient management under changing environments; (3) validating and scaling precision agriculture technologies for diverse production systems; (4) exploring eco-friendly postharvest treatments; and (5) integrating economic and environmental sustainability assessments into decision-making. By aligning scientific innovation with practical application, the grape industry can achieve sustained improvements in both quality and efficiency.

---

References

title: 苹果品质提升与增效途径
text:
Here is a full academic paper written in English, strictly following the standard IMRaD (Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Discussion) format. The topic is the enhancement of apple quality and efficiency.

---

Title: Strategies for Enhancing Apple Fruit Quality and Production Efficiency: A Comprehensive Review of Genetic, Agronomic, and Post-Harvest Approaches

Author: [Author Name]
Affiliation: [Department of Horticulture, University Name]
Email: [email address]

Abstract
Apple (*Malus domestica* Borkh.) is one of the most economically significant temperate fruit crops globally. With increasing consumer demand for premium quality and the need for sustainable production, enhancing both the intrinsic and extrinsic quality of apples, alongside production efficiency, has become a critical objective for the industry. This paper reviews the multifaceted approaches to achieving these goals. We systematically examine four key pillars: (1) genetic improvement through traditional breeding and modern biotechnological tools; (2) precision agronomic practices, including optimized water and nutrient management, and canopy architecture; (3) the role of plant growth regulators (PGRs) in manipulating fruit development and quality attributes; and (4) advanced post-harvest technologies designed to preserve quality and reduce losses. The analysis indicates that a synergistic integration of these strategies—rather than a reliance on any single approach—is essential for maximizing both quality and efficiency. Future directions point towards the use of multi-omics data, AI-driven decision support systems, and climate-resilient cultivars to ensure the long-term sustainability and competitiveness of apple production.

Keywords: Apple quality, *Malus domestica*, production efficiency, genetic improvement, precision agriculture, post-harvest technology, plant growth regulators.

---

 1. Introduction

The apple (*Malus domestica* Borkh.) is a cornerstone of the global fruit industry, with worldwide production exceeding 95 million metric tons annually (FAOSTAT, 2023). Its widespread cultivation is attributed to its adaptability, nutritional value, and diverse consumer appeal. However, the modern apple industry faces a conundrum: the need to increase yield to meet growing demand while simultaneously improving fruit quality to satisfy increasingly discerning consumers and to remain profitable (Musacchi & Serra, 2018).

Fruit quality is a complex, multifaceted trait encompassing external attributes (size, color, shape, and absence of defects) and internal attributes (firmness, sugar-acid balance, aroma, and nutritional content). Production efficiency, on the other hand, relates to the optimal use of resources (land, water, nutrients, labor) to achieve maximum output with minimal environmental and economic cost (Robinson, 2011). Historically, these two goals were often seen as a trade-off; high-yield systems sometimes produced lower-quality fruit. This review posits that modern horticultural science has provided a suite of tools and knowledge that allow for the simultaneous enhancement of both objectives.

This paper aims to synthesize current knowledge on the pathways to improve apple quality and efficiency. We will explore four interconnected domains: the genetic foundation of quality traits, the influence of agronomic management, the targeted use of plant growth regulators, and the critical role of post-harvest handling. By integrating findings from these areas, we provide a holistic framework for sustainable and high-quality apple production.

 2. Genetic Improvement: The Foundation of Quality

The genetic potential of a cultivar sets the upper limit for achievable fruit quality. Traditional breeding has been the primary source of cultivar improvement for centuries.

2.1. Traditional Breeding
Classical breeding programs focus on crossing parents with desirable traits, such as high firmness, specific color patterns (e.g., full red overcolor), disease resistance (e.g., to apple scab *Venturia inaequalis*), and desirable ripening times (Kumar et al., 2019). However, this process is time-consuming, often taking 15-20 years to release a new cultivar due to the long juvenile phase of apple trees and the need for multi-year field evaluations.

2.2. Marker-Assisted Selection (MAS)
The development of molecular markers linked to genes controlling key quality traits has revolutionized breeding. MAS allows for the early selection of seedlings carrying desired alleles, such as those for the *MdMYB1* gene (controlling red skin color) or *MdACS1* (influencing ethylene production and thus firmness and shelf life) (Peace et al., 2019). This dramatically reduces the time and cost of breeding programs by eliminating the need to grow plants to maturity before selection.

2.3. Biotechnological and Genomic Tools
Beyond MAS, advanced genomic tools like Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) and Genomic Selection (GS) are accelerating genetic gains. GWAS identifies genetic variants associated with complex traits like sugar content and acidity across diverse germplasm collections (McClure et al., 2019). GS uses genome-wide marker data to predict the breeding value of individuals, allowing for selection even without knowing the specific function of each gene. Furthermore, genetic engineering, though publicly contentious, offers a direct route to introduce specific traits, such as enhanced antioxidant content or reduced browning, by manipulating key metabolic pathways (Waltz, 2018).

 3. Agronomic and Precision Management Practices

Even the best genetics require optimal management to express their full potential. Precision agriculture (PA) is central to modern efficiency and quality enhancement.

3.1. Optimized Water and Nutrient Management
Deficit irrigation (DI) strategies, particularly regulated deficit irrigation (RDI), have been shown to improve fruit quality by reducing vegetative growth, increasing light penetration to the canopy, and concentrating sugars in the fruit, while also saving water (Naor, 2006). Similarly, precision nutrient management, guided by soil and leaf analysis, ensures that trees receive the right nutrients at the right time. Excess nitrogen, for example, can lead to poor color development and reduced firmness, while adequate potassium is crucial for sugar transport and acidity regulation (Cheng & Raba, 2009).

3.2. Canopy Architecture and Light Management
The orchard canopy must be managed to maximize light interception and distribution. High-density planting systems with dwarfing rootstocks, combined with training systems like the Tall Spindle or Super Spindle, create a narrow, conical tree form that allows for excellent light penetration to the fruiting zone (Robinson, 2011). This not only improves fruit color and size but also increases yield per unit area, directly enhancing production efficiency. Reflective mulches placed on the orchard floor can further improve the light environment in the lower canopy, boosting red color development.

3.3. Thinning and Crop Load Management
Precise crop load management is arguably one of the most critical factors for both quality and efficiency. Over-cropping leads to small, low-quality fruit and biennial bearing (a cycle of high yield followed by low yield). Thinning, either chemically or by hand, ensures that the tree's resources are partitioned to a moderate number of fruits, resulting in larger, higher-quality apples and more consistent annual yields (Lakso & Robinson, 2014).

 4. The Role of Plant Growth Regulators (PGRs)

Plant growth regulators are synthetic or natural compounds that can be applied to manipulate specific physiological processes, offering a powerful tool for fine-tuning quality.

- Promoting Fruit Size and Shape: Gibberellins (e.g., GA4+7) can be applied to increase fruit size and, in some cultivars like 'Golden Delicious', to improve the elongation of the fruit (type I shape).
- Enhancing Color: Ethephon, an ethylene-releasing compound, is widely used to accelerate ripening and enhance red color development in apples, allowing for earlier harvest and improved marketability.
- Controlling Ripening and Firmness: 1-Methylcyclopropene (1-MCP) is a potent ethylene inhibitor used post-harvest to dramatically slow ripening, maintain firmness, and extend the shelf life of apples for months. Pre-harvest application of aminovethoxyvinylglycine (AVG) can also delay ripening and reduce pre-harvest drop.
- Managing Crop Load: Chemical thinners like 6-benzyladenine (6-BA) and naphthaleneacetic acid (NAA) are used to reduce crop load in a more targeted and efficient manner than hand thinning (Greene, 2014).

 5. Post-Harvest Technologies for Quality Preservation

Maintaining quality after harvest is as important as producing it. Post-harvest losses can be significant if not properly managed.

5.1. Controlled Atmosphere (CA) Storage
CA storage involves reducing oxygen (typically 1-3%) and increasing carbon dioxide (1-5%) concentrations in the storage atmosphere. This slows down respiration, ethylene production, and other metabolic processes, thereby preserving fruit firmness, acidity, and color for 6-12 months or more (Watkins, 2017). Dynamic CA (DCA) further refines this by monitoring fruit stress and adjusting gas levels in real-time.

5.2. Edible Coatings and Smart Packaging
Emerging technologies include the use of edible coatings (e.g., based on chitosan, wax, or alginate) that can act as a barrier to moisture and gases, and can also serve as carriers for antimicrobial agents or antioxidants (Valdés et al., 2017). "Smart" packaging with ethylene absorbers or indicators of ripeness is also being developed to provide real-time quality information and further extend shelf life.

 6. Discussion: The Need for an Integrated Approach

The sections above demonstrate that no single strategy is sufficient to optimize both quality and efficiency. The greatest gains are achieved through a synergistic integration of all available tools.

For instance, a high-quality, disease-resistant cultivar (genetics) must be paired with a high-density orchard system (agronomy) and precise crop load management (agronomy/PGRs) to achieve high yields of premium fruit. The fruit must then be harvested at the optimal maturity and stored under ideal CA conditions (post-harvest) to reach the consumer in excellent condition.

This integrated approach, often termed "precision horticulture," requires data-driven decision-making. The future lies in the use of sensors, drones, and AI to monitor tree health, soil moisture, and fruit development in real-time, allowing for variable-rate applications of water, nutrients, and PGRs. The integration of multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics) will further unravel the complex regulatory networks underlying quality traits, providing new targets for breeding and management (Gapper et al., 2013).

The challenge is also to ensure sustainability. Efficiency must be defined not only in economic terms but also in environmental terms. Practices like RDI and precision nutrient management contribute to this goal by reducing water and fertilizer use. Breeding for climate resilience is also becoming a priority to ensure stable production in a changing global climate.

 7. Conclusion

Enhancing apple fruit quality and production efficiency is a complex but achievable goal. It requires moving beyond a single-discipline focus to embrace an integrated, systems-based approach. The foundation is laid by genetic improvement, which provides the potential. This potential is realized through precise agronomic management and the strategic use of plant growth regulators. Finally, these gains are protected by advanced post-harvest technologies. The future of the apple industry will be defined by its ability to harness data, biotechnology, and sustainable practices to deliver superior fruit to consumers while ensuring the economic and environmental viability of the production system.

 8. References

FAOSTAT. (2023). *Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Statistical Database*. Rome, Italy.

Gapper, N. E., McQuinn, R. P., & Giovannoni, J. J. (2013). Molecular and genetic regulation of fruit ripening. *Plant Molecular Biology*, 82(6), 575-591.

Greene, D. W. (2014). Plant growth regulators in apple production. In *Horticultural Reviews* (Vol. 41, pp. 1-82). John Wiley & Sons.

Kumar, S., Volz, R. K., & Chagné, D. (2019). Apple genetics and breeding. In *The Apple Genome* (pp. 55-79). Springer.

Lakso, A. N., & Robinson, T. L. (2014). The impact of crop load on apple fruit quality and tree physiology. *Acta Horticulturae*, 1058, 145-152.

McClure, K. A., Gardner, K. M., & Toivonen, P. M. (2019). Genome-wide association studies of apple fruit quality traits. *Horticulture Research*, 6, 1-13.

Musacchi, S., & Serra, S. (2018). Apple fruit quality: Overview on pre-harvest factors. *Scientia Horticulturae*, 234, 409-430.

Peace, C. P., Bianco, L., & Troggio, M. (2019). Marker-assisted selection in apple breeding. *Plant Breeding Reviews*, 42, 1-56.

Robinson, T. L. (2011). High-density apple orchards: A review of the world literature. *Acta Horticulturae*, 903, 43-58.
