Dobermann, A., Witt, C., Dawe, D., et al. (2002). Site-specific nutrient management for intensive rice cropping systems in Asia. *Field Crops Research*, 74(1), 37–66.

FAO. (2023). *FAOSTAT database*. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations.

Jat, M. L., Chandna, P., Gupta, R., et al. (2019). Laser land leveling: A precursor technology for resource conservation. *Advances in Agronomy*, 156, 1–44.

Yuan, L. P., Wu, L. Q., & Peng, X. S. (2017). Progress in super hybrid rice breeding and cultivation. *Journal of Integrative Agriculture*, 16(12), 2615–2623.

title: 水稻病虫害绿色防控技术
text:
Green Control Technologies for Rice Diseases and Insect Pests: A Comprehensive Review

 Abstract

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) is one of the most important staple food crops worldwide, feeding more than half of the global population. However, rice production is constantly threatened by various diseases and insect pests, causing significant yield losses annually. Traditional chemical control methods, while effective, have led to serious problems including environmental pollution, pesticide resistance, and risks to human health. Green control technologies, which emphasize ecological balance, environmental safety, and sustainable development, have emerged as promising alternatives. This paper provides a comprehensive review of green control technologies for rice diseases and insect pests, including agricultural practices, biological control, physical and mechanical methods, ecological engineering, and integrated pest management (IPM). The challenges and future prospects of these technologies are also discussed. It is concluded that integrating multiple green control strategies within a systems framework is essential for achieving sustainable rice production.

Keywords: rice; diseases and insect pests; green control technology; biological control; integrated pest management; sustainable agriculture

 1. Introduction

Rice is the primary food source for more than 3.5 billion people globally, particularly in Asia, where approximately 90% of the world's rice is produced and consumed (FAO, 2021). China is the largest rice producer and consumer, with rice cultivation covering approximately 30 million hectares annually. However, rice production faces persistent threats from a wide range of diseases and insect pests, including rice blast (Magnaporthe oryzae), bacterial blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae), sheath blight (Rhizoctonia solani), brown planthopper (Nilaparvata lugens), striped stem borer (Chilo suppressalis), and rice leaf folder (Cnaphalocrocis medinalis). These pests and pathogens can cause yield losses ranging from 10% to 30%, and in severe outbreaks, up to 50% or more (Savary et al., 2019).

For decades, chemical pesticides have been the primary means of controlling rice pests and diseases. While these chemicals have contributed significantly to yield stabilization, their overuse has resulted in a series of negative consequences: environmental contamination of soil and water, biodiversity loss, development of pesticide resistance in target organisms, pesticide residues in rice grains, and health risks to farmers and consumers (Tilman et al., 2002). In response to these challenges, the concept of green control (also known as green plant protection) has gained increasing attention worldwide.

Green control technologies refer to a set of environmentally friendly, ecologically sound, and economically viable strategies for managing crop pests and diseases while minimizing reliance on chemical pesticides. The core principles include: (1) prioritizing ecological regulation and natural enemy conservation; (2) using biological and physical methods as primary tools; (3) applying chemical pesticides only as a last resort; and (4) maintaining agricultural ecosystem health and biodiversity (Lu et al., 2022). This paper aims to provide a systematic review of green control technologies for rice diseases and insect pests, covering the major strategies, their mechanisms, application status, and future directions.

 2. Major Rice Diseases and Insect Pests

 2.1 Major Rice Diseases

Rice blast (caused by Magnaporthe oryzae) is one of the most devastating fungal diseases of rice worldwide. It can infect rice at all growth stages, causing leaf blast, node blast, and panicle blast. Panicle blast is particularly destructive, often resulting in complete grain loss. The disease is favored by high humidity, moderate temperatures (24–28°C), and excessive nitrogen fertilization.

Bacterial blight (caused by Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae) is a major bacterial disease in tropical and subtropical rice-growing regions. It causes water-soaked lesions on leaves, leading to wilting and premature death. Yield losses can reach 20–50% in susceptible varieties under favorable conditions.

Sheath blight (caused by Rhizoctonia solani) has become increasingly prevalent with the adoption of high-yielding semi-dwarf varieties and high-density planting. It causes lesions on leaf sheaths and can lead to lodging and significant yield reduction.

Rice false smut (caused by Ustilaginoidea virens) has emerged as a major disease in recent years, particularly in hybrid rice. It not only reduces yield but also produces mycotoxins harmful to human and animal health.

 2.2 Major Rice Insect Pests

Brown planthopper (BPH) (Nilaparvata lugens) is a migratory pest that causes direct damage by sucking plant sap and indirect damage by transmitting viral diseases such as rice ragged stunt virus and rice grassy stunt virus. BPH outbreaks can cause "hopperburn," resulting in complete crop failure.

Striped stem borer (Chilo suppressalis) larvae bore into rice stems, causing dead hearts at the vegetative stage and white heads at the reproductive stage. It is a major pest in temperate rice-growing regions.

Rice leaf folder (Cnaphalocrocis medinalis) larvae fold rice leaves and feed on the mesophyll, reducing photosynthetic area and causing significant yield losses during severe outbreaks.

Rice planthoppers (including Sogatella furcifera and Laodelphax striatellus) and rice water weevil (Lissorhoptrus oryzophilus) are also important pests in various regions.

 3. Green Control Technologies

 3.1 Agricultural Control

Agricultural control involves manipulating cultivation practices to create unfavorable conditions for pests and diseases while promoting rice growth and vigor. Key measures include:

Resistant variety deployment: The use of disease-resistant and pest-resistant rice varieties is the most economical and effective green control strategy. Breeding programs have developed varieties carrying resistance genes such as Pi9, Pi2, and Pita for blast resistance; Xa4, Xa7, and Xa21 for bacterial blight resistance; and Bph14 and Bph15 for brown planthopper resistance (Jiang et al., 2020). However, resistance can be overcome by pathogen/pest evolution, necessitating continuous monitoring and gene rotation.

Rational fertilization: Excessive nitrogen application increases susceptibility to blast, sheath blight, and brown planthopper. Balanced fertilization with appropriate nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium ratios and silicon supplementation enhances plant resistance. Silicon application, in particular, has been shown to strengthen cell walls and improve resistance to multiple pests and diseases.

Water management: Alternate wetting and drying (AWD) irrigation reduces sheath blight severity and suppresses brown planthopper populations while saving water. Proper drainage during peak pest periods can also reduce pest abundance.

Crop rotation and intercropping: Rotating rice with other crops breaks pest and disease cycles. Intercropping rice with trap crops or banker plants can attract natural enemies and reduce pest populations.

Field sanitation: Removing crop residues, weed hosts, and volunteer rice plants reduces overwintering sites for pests and pathogens.

 3.2 Biological Control

Biological control utilizes living organisms to suppress pest and disease populations. It is a cornerstone of green control technology.

Natural enemy conservation and augmentation: Rice ecosystems harbor rich biodiversity of natural enemies, including predatory spiders, mirid bugs (Cyrtorhinus lividipennis), lady beetles, and parasitic wasps (e.g., Trichogramma spp., Anagrus spp.). Conservation biological control through habitat management, reduced pesticide use, and provision of refuge areas can enhance natural enemy populations and their pest suppression capacity. Augmentative releases of Trichogramma wasps have been widely used against rice stem borers, achieving control efficacy comparable to chemical pesticides (Guo et al., 2021).

Microbial pesticides: Several microbial agents have been developed and commercialized for rice pest and disease control. Bacillus subtilis and Bacillus cereus are effective against rice blast and sheath blight. Trichoderma spp. are used for soil-borne disease control. Beauveria bassiana and Metarhizium anisopliae are entomopathogenic fungi effective against planthoppers and stem borers. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) formulations target lepidopteran pests.

Botanical pesticides: Plant-derived compounds such as azadirachtin (from neem), rotenone, and matrine have insecticidal and antifungal properties. These biopesticides are biodegradable, safe for non-target organisms, and less prone to resistance development.

Viral insecticides: Nuclear polyhedrosis viruses (NPVs) specific to rice stem borers have been developed as bioinsecticides. They are highly specific, safe, and can cause epizootics in pest populations.

Antagonistic microorganisms: Rhizosphere bacteria and fungi can induce systemic resistance in rice plants. For example, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Burkholderia spp. have been shown to trigger defense responses against blast and bacterial blight.

 3.3 Physical and Mechanical Control

Physical and mechanical methods use non-chemical means to directly kill or remove pests.

Light traps: Blacklight and LED traps are widely used to monitor and mass-trap nocturnal rice pests such as stem borers, leaf folders, and planthoppers. These traps exploit the phototactic behavior of insects and can significantly reduce pest populations when deployed at appropriate densities.

Sex pheromone traps: Synthetic sex pheromones are used for monitoring and mating disruption of stem borers and leaf folders. Pheromone traps are species-specific, environmentally safe, and effective at low pest densities.

Yellow sticky traps: Yellow-colored sticky boards attract and capture planthoppers, leafhoppers, and other small flying insects. They are particularly useful for early-season monitoring and suppression.

Physical barriers: Fine mesh screens or nets can exclude pests from seedbeds and nurseries. This is particularly effective for preventing viral disease transmission by insect vectors.

Thermal and radiation treatments: Hot water treatment of seeds can eliminate seed-borne pathogens. Gamma irradiation is used for quarantine purposes and sterility induction in some pest management programs.

 3.4 Ecological Engineering

Ecological engineering approaches aim to redesign agricultural landscapes to enhance ecosystem services, particularly natural pest control and pollination.

Habitat management: Planting flowering plants (e.g., sesame, sunflower, buckwheat) along rice field margins provides nectar and pollen for adult parasitoids and predators, enhancing their survival and reproduction. This "flowers on the edges" strategy has been widely adopted in China and other Asian countries (Lu et al., 2022).

Banker plant systems: Non-crop plants that harbor alternative prey or hosts for natural enemies can be established near rice fields. For example, planting vetiver grass or sorghum as banker plants can support populations of predatory mirid bugs and spiders.

Landscape diversification: Maintaining non-rice habitats such as ponds, hedgerows, and fallow fields within agricultural landscapes promotes biodiversity and biological control. Landscape-level planning can reduce pest outbreaks by conserving natural enemy metapopulations.

Rice-fish and rice-duck co-culture: Integrating fish or ducks into rice paddies creates a multi-trophic system where fish/ducks feed on pests, weeds, and algae while providing nutrients through their waste. This traditional practice has been revived and scientifically optimized as a green control technology. Studies have shown that rice-fish co-culture can reduce planthopper and leaf folder populations by 30–60% (Xie et al., 2011).

 3.5 Integrated Pest Management (IPM)

IPM is a decision-making framework that combines multiple control tactics based on ecological principles and economic thresholds. For rice, IPM typically includes:

1. Monitoring and forecasting: Regular field scouting and pheromone/light trap monitoring to assess pest and disease incidence. Disease forecasting models based on weather data (temperature, humidity, rainfall) help predict blast and bacterial blight outbreaks.

2. Economic threshold levels (ETL): Control measures are initiated only when pest populations exceed predetermined thresholds that justify intervention. This avoids unnecessary pesticide applications.

3. Combination of tactics: Cultural, biological, physical, and chemical methods are integrated in a compatible manner. For example, resistant varieties + natural enemy conservation + pheromone traps + targeted biopesticide application.

4. Selective and reduced-risk pesticides: When chemical control is necessary, selective insecticides (e.g., buprofezin, pymetrozine) that are less harmful to natural enemies are preferred over broad-spectrum chemicals. Seed treatment and granule application are preferred over foliar sprays to reduce environmental impact.

5. Post-harvest management: Proper storage and sanitation reduce carryover of pests and pathogens to the next season.

 4. Case Studies and Application Status

 4.1 China's Green Control Initiative

Since 2015, China's Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs has implemented the "Zero Growth of Chemical Fertilizer and Pesticide Use" action plan, later upgraded to the "Green Control of Pests and Diseases" program. By 2022, green control technologies were applied on more than 60 million hectares of rice fields, reducing chemical pesticide use by over 20% compared to 2015 levels. Key measures include:

- Large-scale release of Trichogramma wasps for stem borer control in Northeast China
- Rice-fish co-culture in Southwest China (Guizhou, Yunnan, Sichuan)
- Rice-duck co-culture in South China (Hunan, Guangdong)
- Pheromone trap networks for monitoring and mass trapping
- Ecological engineering with flowering plants in field margins

 4.2 Japan's Eco-Friendly Rice Farming

Japan has promoted "eco-friendly rice farming" since the 1990s, with certification systems for reduced-pesticide rice. Key technologies include:

- Use of resistant varieties and reduced pesticide application
- Rice-duck and rice-fish co-culture
- Habitat management for natural enemies
- Biological pesticides (Bt, Beauveria bassiana)

 4.3 Southeast Asian Experiences

In Vietnam, the "Three Reductions, Three Gains" program (reducing seed, fertilizer, and pesticide use) has been widely adopted, improving both profitability and environmental sustainability. In the Philippines, the "PalayCheck" system integrates best management practices including IPM. In Thailand, the "Good Agricultural Practices" (GAP) program promotes green control for export-oriented rice production.

 5. Challenges and Limitations

Despite the promise of green control technologies, several challenges limit their widespread adoption:

Efficacy variability: Biological control agents and botanical pesticides often have lower and more variable efficacy than chemical pesticides, particularly during severe pest outbreaks. Environmental factors (temperature, humidity, UV radiation) can affect their performance.

Slow action: Many green control measures (e.g., natural enemy conservation, habitat management) require time to establish and may not provide immediate control during acute pest emergencies.

Knowledge and training: Green control technologies are knowledge-intensive and require farmers to understand pest ecology, natural enemy biology, and decision-making thresholds. This demands substantial investment in extension and training.

Economic constraints: Some green control methods (e.g., pheromone traps, microbial pesticides) may be more expensive than conventional chemicals in the short term, although they are often more cost-effective in the long run.

Scalability: Ecological engineering approaches that work well at small scales may be difficult to implement across large, homogeneous landscapes.

Regulatory and policy support: In many countries, regulatory frameworks and subsidies still favor chemical pesticides. Policy support for green control is essential for widespread adoption.

Climate change: Changing climate patterns may alter pest and disease dynamics, potentially reducing the effectiveness of current green control strategies and requiring adaptive management.

 6. Future Prospects

The future of green control for rice pests and diseases lies in the integration of traditional ecological knowledge with modern biotechnology and digital agriculture. Promising directions include:

Genomic and breeding advances: CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing and marker-assisted selection can accelerate the development of multi-resistant rice varieties. Understanding the molecular basis of plant-pathogen interactions will enable more durable resistance.

Microbiome engineering: Manipulating the rice microbiome (phyllosphere, rhizosphere, endosphere) to enhance disease suppression and pest resistance is a frontier area of research.

RNA interference (RNAi): Spray-induced gene silencing (SIGS) using dsRNA targeting essential pest genes offers a species-specific, environmentally safe control method.

Digital and precision agriculture: Remote sensing, drones, and IoT sensors can enable real-time monitoring of pest and disease outbreaks, precision application of biopesticides, and data-driven decision support for farmers.

AI and machine learning: Image recognition and machine learning algorithms can automate pest and disease identification, improving early detection and response.

Synthetic biology: Engineering microorganisms to produce novel biopesticides or enhance natural enemy performance.

Climate-smart IPM

title: 番茄养殖技术与效益分析
text:
Here is a short academic paper on the requested topic, written in English and following the standard academic format.

---

 Tomato Cultivation Techniques and Profitability Analysis: A Review

Author: [Author's Name]
Affiliation: [Author's Institution/Department]
Email: [Author's Email]

---

 Abstract

Tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum*) is one of the most significant and widely consumed vegetable crops globally. Its production is a major agricultural activity, contributing substantially to the economies of many nations and the livelihoods of farmers. However, the profitability of tomato cultivation is highly dependent on the adoption of optimal agricultural practices and a clear understanding of market dynamics. This paper provides a concise review of modern tomato cultivation techniques, including variety selection, soil management, and advanced greenhouse production systems. It then presents a framework for analyzing the profitability of tomato farming, examining key factors such as input costs, labor, yield, and market price volatility. The analysis reveals that while advanced techniques like greenhouse cultivation can significantly increase yields and enable off-season production, they also demand higher capital investment. Therefore, the economic viability of a tomato farming operation hinges on a strategic balance between technological investment, operational efficiency, and effective market access. This paper concludes that a holistic approach, integrating technical proficiency with sound economic planning, is essential for maximizing the profitability and sustainability of tomato production.

Keywords: Tomato Cultivation, *Solanum lycopersicum*, Agricultural Technology, Profitability Analysis, Greenhouse Farming, Cost-Benefit Analysis

---

 1. Introduction

The tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum*) is a staple in global diets and a high-value cash crop for millions of farmers worldwide (FAO, 2021). Its cultivation spans diverse agro-climatic zones, from open-field systems in temperate regions to sophisticated, climate-controlled greenhouses. The global demand for tomatoes, both fresh and processed, continues to rise, driven by population growth and changing dietary habits. This increasing demand presents significant economic opportunities for producers.

However, tomato production is fraught with challenges, including pest and disease pressure, climate variability, and significant post-harvest losses. Furthermore, market prices for tomatoes are notoriously volatile, creating substantial economic risk for growers. In this context, the success of a tomato farming enterprise is not solely determined by the quantity of produce but by the net profit it generates. This requires a dual focus: the mastery of modern cultivation techniques to optimize yield and quality, and a rigorous analysis of the associated costs and revenues.

This paper aims to provide a structured overview of contemporary tomato cultivation techniques and to establish a framework for analyzing the profitability of such operations. It seeks to answer the following questions: What are the key technological and management practices driving modern tomato production? And what are the primary economic factors that determine the financial success of a tomato farm? By synthesizing information on both production and economics, this paper offers a comprehensive perspective for current and prospective tomato growers, as well as for agricultural policymakers and researchers.

 2. Modern Tomato Cultivation Techniques

The optimization of tomato yield and quality relies on a systematic approach to cultivation, encompassing several key stages.

2.1. Variety Selection and Seedling Management
The choice of tomato variety is the foundational decision, determined by the target market (fresh consumption vs. processing), desired fruit characteristics (size, color, flavor), and resistance to local pests and diseases. Modern breeding has produced a vast array of hybrid varieties offering high yields, disease resistance (e.g., to Fusarium and Verticillium wilt), and improved fruit quality. Healthy seedling production in a controlled nursery environment is critical for ensuring uniform field establishment and vigorous early growth.

2.2. Soil and Nutrient Management
Tomatoes thrive in well-drained, loamy soils rich in organic matter, with an optimal pH range of 6.0 to 6.8. A comprehensive soil test is essential to determine nutrient deficiencies and guide fertilization. The application of organic matter (e.g., compost or manure) improves soil structure, water-holding capacity, and microbial activity. Inorganic fertilizers are then applied to meet the specific macronutrient (Nitrogen, Phosphorus, Potassium) and micronutrient needs of the crop throughout its growth cycle. The use of drip irrigation systems allows for the precise application of water and nutrients directly to the root zone (fertigation), significantly improving resource-use efficiency.

2.3. Environmental Control and Protected Cultivation
While open-field cultivation is common, protected cultivation in greenhouses or high tunnels offers significant advantages. These structures allow for greater control over the growing environment, protecting plants from adverse weather, extending the growing season, and enabling off-season production, which often commands higher market prices. In advanced greenhouse systems, temperature, humidity, and carbon dioxide (CO2) levels can be meticulously managed to optimize photosynthesis and plant development. Soilless culture (hydroponics) is another advanced technique where plants are grown in an inert medium (e.g., rockwool, coco coir) and supplied with a balanced nutrient solution, offering precise control and avoiding soil-borne diseases.

2.4. Integrated Pest and Disease Management (IPM)
A robust IPM strategy is crucial for minimizing crop losses and reducing reliance on chemical pesticides. IPM combines biological control (introducing natural predators), cultural practices (crop rotation, sanitation), physical controls (mulching, trellising), and the strategic, targeted use of approved pesticides only when economic thresholds are reached.

 3. Profitability Analysis Framework

The profitability of tomato cultivation can be assessed through a standard cost-benefit analysis, which calculates the net profit by subtracting total costs from total revenue.

3.1. Cost Structure
The total cost of production can be divided into two main categories:

- Fixed Costs: These are costs that do not vary with the level of production. They include land rent or mortgage, depreciation on farm machinery and greenhouse structures, and insurance.
- Variable Costs: These are costs that are directly tied to the scale of production. They include:
    - Inputs: Seeds/seedlings, fertilizers, pesticides, and growing media.
    - Labor: Costs for planting, pruning, trellising, harvesting, and packing. Labor can represent a significant portion of total costs.
    - Energy: Electricity for greenhouse heating, cooling, and lighting, and fuel for machinery.
    - Other: Water, packaging materials, and transportation.

3.2. Revenue Generation
Total revenue is a function of two primary factors: yield (total quantity harvested) and market price per unit. Yield is heavily influenced by the cultivation techniques discussed above. Market price is determined by supply and demand dynamics, which are affected by seasonality, produce quality, and market access channels (e.g., direct-to-consumer, wholesale, or processing contracts).

3.3. Key Profitability Indicators
- Net Profit: Total Revenue - Total Costs
- Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR): Total Revenue / Total Costs. A BCR greater than 1 indicates profitability.
- Break-Even Point: The level of production (yield) or revenue at which total costs are covered.

 4. Discussion: Integrating Technique and Economics

The relationship between cultivation techniques and profitability is direct and multifaceted. Adopting advanced techniques is an investment decision. For instance, transitioning from open-field to greenhouse production requires a high initial capital investment and increased operational costs (especially for energy). However, this investment can be justified by:

1.  Increased Yield and Quality: Greenhouse environments can produce 5-10 times the yield of open-field systems per unit area and provide premium-quality fruit.
2.  Off-Season Premium Pricing: The ability to supply tomatoes during off-season periods when market supply is low can lead to significantly higher prices, boosting revenue.
3.  Risk Mitigation: Protected cultivation reduces the risk of crop failure due to extreme weather events or pest outbreaks, providing more stable and predictable income.

Conversely, even in open-field systems, the adoption of efficient techniques like drip irrigation and IPM can reduce variable costs (water, fertilizer, pesticides) and increase marketable yield, thereby improving the benefit-cost ratio without massive capital outlay. The optimal strategy depends on the specific context—available capital, market demand, and local climate. A thorough market analysis is as crucial as agronomic expertise; producing a high-value crop is futile if there is no profitable market to sell it to.

 5. Conclusion

The cultivation of tomatoes offers a viable and potentially lucrative agricultural enterprise. However, achieving sustained profitability requires more than just good farming practices. It demands a strategic integration of advanced cultivation techniques with rigorous economic analysis. Modern techniques, particularly those involving protected cultivation and precision agriculture, offer pathways to higher yields and premium markets but come with increased costs and management complexity.

The profitability of any tomato farming operation is ultimately determined by the delicate balance between the investment in technology and the realized returns from the market. Therefore, successful growers are those who function as both skilled agronomists and savvy business managers. They must continuously evaluate new technologies, manage costs efficiently, and adapt their marketing strategies to navigate the volatile agricultural marketplace. Future research should focus on developing cost-effective sustainable production systems and improving market intelligence to help farmers make more informed decisions and enhance the resilience and profitability of the tomato industry.

---

 References

Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). (2021). *FAOSTAT Database*. Rome, Italy: FAO.

Heuvelink, E. (Ed.). (2018). *Tomatoes*. CABI.

Jones, J. B. (2014). *Tomato Plant Culture: In the Field, Greenhouse, and Home Garden* (3rd ed.). CRC Press.

title: 大蒜种植增收增产技术分析
text:
Title: Analysis of Techniques for Increasing Yield and Income in Garlic Cultivation

Abstract:
Garlic (Allium sativum L.) is a globally significant vegetable and condiment crop. Enhancing its yield and economic return is crucial for growers. This paper analyzes key agronomic and management techniques that contribute to increased garlic production and income. These include optimized variety selection, scientific fertilization, precise irrigation, integrated pest and disease management, and improved post-harvest handling. The analysis indicates that adopting a comprehensive technical package can significantly raise both bulb yield and market value, thereby increasing net income for farmers. The findings provide a practical reference for sustainable garlic production.

Keywords: garlic; yield increase; income improvement; cultivation techniques; agronomic management

1. Introduction
Garlic is valued for its flavor, medicinal properties, and nutritional benefits. Global demand continues to rise. However, many smallholder growers achieve suboptimal yields due to traditional practices, leading to low economic returns. Improving cultivation techniques is therefore essential to meet market demand and enhance rural livelihoods. This paper reviews and analyzes proven methods for increasing garlic yield and income, focusing on practical field-level interventions.

2. Key Techniques for Yield and Income Enhancement

2.1 Variety Selection and Seed Treatment
Choosing high-yielding, disease-resistant, and market-preferred varieties adapted to local climate is the first step. Certified disease-free seed cloves should be used. Treating seed cloves with fungicides or bio-agents before planting reduces soil-borne diseases and improves germination uniformity, leading to stronger early growth.

2.2 Soil Preparation and Planting Density
Garlic prefers well-drained, loamy soil rich in organic matter with pH 6.0–7.0. Deep plowing and thorough harrowing create a fine seedbed. Optimal planting density varies by variety and region; generally, 200,000–300,000 plants per hectare are recommended. Proper spacing ensures adequate light, air, and nutrient availability, reducing competition and boosting bulb size.

2.3 Scientific Fertilization
Balanced fertilization based on soil testing is critical. Garlic has high demands for nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and sulfur. Applying well-decomposed organic manure (e.g., 20–30 t/ha) improves soil structure and fertility. Synthetic fertilizers should be split-applied: basal application before planting, top-dressing during vegetative growth, and bulb enlargement stages. Sulfur enhances pungency and bulb quality. Avoiding excessive nitrogen prevents lodging and disease susceptibility.

2.4 Irrigation Management
Garlic requires consistent moisture but is sensitive to waterlogging. Drip irrigation or furrow irrigation with proper drainage is recommended. Critical watering periods include planting, vegetative growth, and bulb bulbing. Reducing irrigation before harvest improves bulb storage quality and prevents splitting.

2.5 Integrated Pest and Disease Management (IPDM)
Common pests include thrips, mites, and nematodes; major diseases are white rot, downy mildew, and rust. IPDM combines cultural practices (crop rotation, sanitation, resistant varieties), biological control (e.g., Trichoderma), and judicious chemical use only when thresholds are exceeded. This reduces yield losses and pesticide costs, increasing net income.

2.6 Weed Control
Weeds compete for nutrients and water. Mulching with straw or plastic film suppresses weeds, conserves moisture, and moderates soil temperature. Pre-emergence herbicides can be used carefully, but manual weeding during early growth is often necessary for high-value crops.

2.7 Harvesting and Post-Harvest Handling
Timely harvest when lower leaves turn yellow and bulbs are firm prevents over-maturity and bulb splitting. Proper curing (drying) in a well-ventilated shaded area for 1–2 weeks reduces moisture content, extends shelf life, and maintains quality. Grading and attractive packaging increase market price. Value addition (e.g., processing into paste, powder) can further raise income.

3. Economic Analysis
Adopting the above techniques increases yield from a traditional 8–10 t/ha to 15–20 t/ha. With improved quality, market price may rise by 20–30%. Although input costs (certified seeds, fertilizers, drip system) increase, the net income typically doubles or triples due to higher yield and premium prices. Government subsidies and cooperative marketing can further enhance profitability.

4. Conclusion
Increasing garlic yield and income requires an integrated approach combining improved varieties, precision fertilization, efficient irrigation, IPDM, and proper post-harvest management. These techniques are technically feasible and economically viable for small and large farms. Extension services should promote farmer training and demonstration plots to accelerate adoption. Future research should focus on climate-resilient varieties and smart farming technologies.

References
[1] Smith, J. et al. (2020). *Garlic Production Guide*. FAO.
[2] Zhang, L. & Wang, H. (2019). Effects of sulfur fertilization on garlic yield and quality. *Journal of Horticultural Science*, 45(3), 210–218.
[3] Kumar, S. & Singh, R. (2021). Integrated pest management in allium crops. *Crop Protection*, 32(4), 301–309.
[4] Local Agricultural Extension Bulletin (2022). Garlic Cultivation for Higher Income.

title: 水稻标准化生产技术
text:
Standardized Production Technology for Rice: A Comprehensive Framework for Sustainable and High-Yield Cultivation

 Abstract

Rice (Oryza sativa L.) serves as a staple food for more than half of the world's population, making its production efficiency and sustainability critical to global food security. Standardized production technology (SPT) has emerged as a systematic approach to optimizing rice cultivation through the integration of scientific research, technological innovation, and practical field management. This paper presents a comprehensive review of standardized production technologies for rice, covering key aspects including variety selection, seed treatment, nursery management, field preparation, water and fertilizer management, pest and disease control, and mechanized harvesting. The implementation of standardized protocols has demonstrated significant improvements in yield, resource use efficiency, and grain quality while reducing environmental impacts. Challenges and future directions for the widespread adoption of standardized rice production systems are also discussed.

Keywords: rice; standardized production technology; sustainable agriculture; yield improvement; resource use efficiency; integrated crop management

 1. Introduction

Rice is one of the most important cereal crops globally, feeding approximately 3.5 billion people and providing 20% of the world's dietary energy supply (FAO, 2022). With the global population projected to reach 9.7 billion by 2050, rice production must increase by 25–30% to meet future demand (Seck et al., 2012). However, this challenge is compounded by shrinking arable land, water scarcity, climate change, and increasing labor costs.

Traditional rice farming practices often suffer from inconsistencies in management, leading to variable yields, inefficient resource utilization, and environmental degradation. Standardized production technology (SPT) offers a systematic solution by establishing uniform, science-based protocols for all stages of rice cultivation. These protocols are designed to maximize yield potential while minimizing inputs, ensuring consistency, and promoting sustainability.

This paper aims to: (1) define the concept and principles of standardized rice production technology; (2) describe the key components of standardized protocols across the rice production cycle; (3) evaluate the benefits and challenges of standardization; and (4) propose future directions for research and extension.

 2. Concept and Principles of Standardized Production Technology

 2.1 Definition

Standardized production technology refers to a set of scientifically validated, systematically organized, and practically applicable procedures that govern agricultural production processes. For rice, SPT encompasses all operations from land preparation to post-harvest handling, with each step defined by specific technical parameters, timing, and quality criteria.

 2.2 Core Principles

1. Scientific basis: All protocols are derived from rigorous research in agronomy, plant physiology, soil science, and agricultural engineering.
2. Systematic integration: Individual practices are integrated into a coherent system, ensuring synergy among components.
3. Reproducibility: Standardized procedures yield consistent results across different environments and seasons.
4. Sustainability: Protocols prioritize long-term soil health, water conservation, and biodiversity.
5. Scalability: Standards are designed for adoption at various scales, from smallholder farms to large commercial operations.
6. Adaptability: While standardized, protocols allow for regional adaptation based on local climate, soil, and socio-economic conditions.

 3. Key Components of Standardized Rice Production Technology

 3.1 Variety Selection and Seed Treatment

Variety selection is the foundation of standardized rice production. Recommended varieties should possess:
- High yield potential and stability
- Resistance or tolerance to major pests and diseases
- Appropriate growth duration for the target cropping system
- Desirable grain quality traits (e.g., milling recovery, appearance, cooking quality)
- Tolerance to abiotic stresses (drought, salinity, submergence)

Seed treatment protocols include:
- Seed cleaning and grading to ensure uniform size and vigor
- Disinfection using hot water treatment (60°C for 10 minutes) or approved fungicides to prevent seed-borne diseases
- Seed priming to enhance germination uniformity and seedling vigor
- Seed coating with nutrients or biological agents where appropriate

 3.2 Nursery Management

Standardized nursery management ensures healthy, uniform seedlings:

- Seedbed preparation: Raised beds with fine, level soil; proper drainage channels
- Sowing density: 30–40 g of seeds per m² for conventional transplanting; adjusted for mechanical transplanting
- Water management: Shallow irrigation during germination; controlled water levels thereafter
- Temperature control: Protection from cold stress using plastic covers when necessary
- Seedling age: Transplanting at 3–4 leaf stage (18–25 days) for optimal establishment
- Hardening: Gradual exposure to field conditions before transplanting

 3.3 Field Preparation and Crop Establishment

Land preparation standards include:
- Plowing to a depth of 15–20 cm followed by harrowing
- Leveling within ±3 cm to ensure uniform water distribution
- Incorporation of organic matter and basal fertilizers
- Construction of appropriate bunds and water inlets/outlets

Crop establishment methods:
- Mechanical transplanting: Standardized spacing of 30 cm × 12–15 cm, 2–3 seedlings per hill
- Direct seeding: Precise seeding rates (40–60 kg/ha) with uniform distribution
- System of Rice Intensification (SRI): Single seedling per hill at wider spacing (25 cm × 25 cm) for specific contexts

 3.4 Water Management

Standardized water management protocols promote water use efficiency:

- Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD): Irrigation applied when water level drops to 15 cm below soil surface; reduces water use by 25–30% without yield penalty
- Controlled irrigation: Maintaining shallow water (3–5 cm) during critical growth stages (tillering, panicle initiation, flowering)
- Mid-season drainage: Draining fields for 7–10 days at maximum tillering to control ineffective tillers and improve root aeration
- Deficit irrigation: Regulated water stress during non-critical stages

 3.5 Nutrient Management

Standardized fertilization is based on soil testing and crop demand:

- Site-specific nutrient management (SSNM): Fertilizer rates adjusted based on indigenous nutrient supply, yield target, and recovery efficiency
- Recommended doses (for a 6 t/ha target):
  - Nitrogen (N): 120–150 kg/ha, split into 3–4 applications
  - Phosphorus (P₂O₅): 60–80 kg/ha, applied as basal
  - Potassium (K₂O): 80–100 kg/ha, split into 2 applications
  - Zinc (Zn): 5–10 kg/ha where deficiency occurs
- Application timing: Basal (50% P, 30% K), tillering (30% N), panicle initiation (40% N, 40% K), flowering (30% N, 30% K)
- Organic amendments: Incorporation of green manure, straw, or compost to maintain soil organic matter

 3.6 Pest and Disease Management

Standardized Integrated Pest Management (IPM) protocols include:

- Monitoring and forecasting: Regular field scouting; use of light traps and pheromone traps
- Economic threshold levels: Treatment initiated only when pest populations exceed thresholds
- Biological control: Conservation of natural enemies (spiders, parasitic wasps); release of Trichogramma for stem borer control
- Cultural practices: Resistant varieties, crop rotation, synchronous planting, removal of weed hosts
- Chemical control: Judicious use of approved pesticides at recommended doses; rotation of modes of action to prevent resistance
- Major pests and diseases addressed:
  - Insect pests: stem borers, brown planthopper, leaf folder, gall midge
  - Diseases: blast, bacterial blight, sheath blight, tungro virus

 3.7 Weed Management

- Pre-planting: Clean field preparation; stale seedbed technique
- Pre-emergence herbicides: Application within 3 days of transplanting/sowing
- Post-emergence herbicides: Targeted application at 2–4 leaf stage of weeds
- Mechanical control: Use of rotary weeders in SRI systems
- Water management: Maintaining shallow water to suppress weed germination

 3.8 Mechanized Harvesting and Post-Harvest Handling

- Harvest timing: When 85–90% of grains are straw-colored; grain moisture at 20–25%
- Mechanical harvesting: Combine harvesters with standardized settings for minimal grain loss (<3%)
- Threshing and cleaning: Mechanical threshers with appropriate drum speed (500–600 rpm)
- Drying: Mechanical dryers or sun drying to reduce moisture to 14% for safe storage
- Storage: Hermetic storage systems to prevent insect infestation and mold growth
- Milling: Standardized milling procedures to maximize head rice recovery (>60%)

 4. Benefits of Standardized Production Technology

 4.1 Yield Improvement

Studies across major rice-producing regions have demonstrated that SPT adoption increases yields by 10–25% compared to traditional practices (Peng et al., 2010). This improvement results from optimized plant density, balanced nutrition, timely operations, and reduced losses from pests and diseases.

 4.2 Resource Use Efficiency

- Water: AWD reduces irrigation water use by 25–30%
- Fertilizer: SSNM improves nitrogen use efficiency by 15–20%
- Labor: Mechanization reduces labor requirements by 40–60%
- Land: Improved cropping intensity through timely operations

 4.3 Quality Consistency

Standardized protocols ensure uniform grain quality, meeting market specifications for milling, appearance, and cooking properties. This consistency enhances market access and price premiums for farmers.

 4.4 Environmental Sustainability

- Reduced greenhouse gas emissions (methane) through AWD
- Lower chemical pollution through IPM and judicious fertilizer use
- Improved soil health through organic matter management
- Conservation of biodiversity through reduced pesticide applications

 4.5 Climate Resilience

Standardized protocols incorporating stress-tolerant varieties and adaptive water management enhance resilience to drought, flooding, and temperature extremes.

 5. Challenges and Constraints

 5.1 Adoption Barriers

- Smallholder fragmentation: Small farm sizes complicate mechanization and uniform management
- Knowledge gaps: Limited access to training and extension services
- Financial constraints: Initial investment costs for mechanization and inputs
- Risk aversion: Farmer reluctance to deviate from traditional practices

 5.2 Regional Adaptation

Standardized protocols must be calibrated for local conditions, including climate, soil type, water availability, and socio-economic context. A "one-size-fits-all" approach is neither feasible nor desirable.

 5.3 Infrastructure Limitations

- Inadequate irrigation and drainage systems
- Poor rural roads and market access
- Limited availability of quality seeds and inputs
- Insufficient drying and storage facilities

 5.4 Institutional and Policy Issues

- Weak extension systems
- Lack of quality control and certification mechanisms
- Inconsistent government policies on subsidies and pricing
- Limited public-private partnerships

 6. Future Directions

 6.1 Digital Agriculture and Precision Farming

Integration of remote sensing, GPS-guided machinery, and decision support systems can enhance the precision and efficiency of standardized protocols. Smartphone-based apps can deliver real-time advisories to farmers.

 6.2 Climate-Smart Standardization

Developing standardized protocols that explicitly incorporate climate resilience—such as drought-tolerant varieties, water-saving technologies, and diversified cropping systems—will be essential.

 6.3 Participatory Standard Development

Engaging farmers in the co-development and validation of standards ensures relevance and enhances adoption. Farmer field schools and participatory variety selection are effective mechanisms.

 6.4 Public-Private Partnerships

Collaboration among government agencies, research institutions, private companies, and farmer organizations can accelerate the development, dissemination, and adoption of standardized technologies.

 6.5 Policy Support

Governments should invest in:
- Extension and training programs
- Infrastructure development (irrigation, roads, storage)
- Quality seed systems
- Market linkages and price stabilization
- Incentives for sustainable practices

 7. Conclusion

Standardized production technology represents a comprehensive and systematic approach to rice cultivation that integrates scientific knowledge, technological innovation, and practical field management. By establishing uniform protocols for variety selection, crop establishment, water and nutrient management, pest control, and post-harvest handling, SPT enables farmers to achieve higher yields, better quality, and improved resource use efficiency while reducing environmental impacts.

The successful adoption of standardized rice production technology requires addressing challenges related to smallholder fragmentation, knowledge dissemination, infrastructure, and policy support. Future efforts should focus on digital integration, climate resilience, participatory approaches, and multi-stakeholder collaboration. With appropriate investment and institutional support, standardized production technology can play a pivotal role in ensuring global food security and agricultural sustainability in the 21st century.

 References

1. FAO. (2022). *World Food and Agriculture – Statistical Yearbook 2022*. Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, Rome.

2. Seck, P.A., Diagne, A., Mohanty, S., & Wopereis, M.C.S. (2012). Crops that feed the world 7: Rice. *Food Security*, 4(1), 7–24.

3. Peng, S., Buresh, R.J., Huang, J., et al. (2010). Improving nitrogen fertilization in rice by site-specific N management: A review. *Agronomy for Sustainable Development*, 30(3), 649–656.

4. Bouman, B.A.M., Lampayan, R.M., & Tuong, T.P. (2007). *Water Management in Irrigated Rice: Coping with Water Scarcity*. International Rice Research Institute, Los Baños, Philippines.

5. Dobermann, A., & Fairhurst, T. (2000). *Rice: Nutrient Disorders and Nutrient Management*. Potash & Phosphate Institute, Singapore.

6. Savary, S., Willocquet, L., Elazegui, F.A., et al. (2000). Rice pest constraints in tropical Asia: Quantification of yield losses due to rice pests in a range of production situations. *Plant Disease*, 84(3), 357–369.

7. Uphoff, N., Kassam, A., & Harwood, R. (2011). SRI as a methodology for raising crop and water productivity: Productive adaptations in rice agronomy and irrigation water management. *Paddy and Water Environment*, 9(1), 3–11.

8. Chauhan, B.S., & Johnson, D.E. (2010). The role of seed ecology in improving weed management strategies in the tropics. *Advances in Agronomy*, 105, 221–262.

9. IRRI. (2015). *Rice Knowledge Bank: Standardized Production Protocols*. International Rice Research Institute, Los Baños, Philippines.

10. Zhang, F., Chen, X., & Vitousek, P. (2013). Chinese agriculture: An experiment for the world. *Nature*, 497(7447), 33–35.

title: 玉米品质提升与增效途径
text:
Approaches to Quality Improvement and Efficiency Enhancement in Maize: A Review

 Abstract

Maize (*Zea mays* L.) is one of the world's most important cereal crops, serving as a staple food, livestock feed, and industrial raw material. With the growing global demand for food security and sustainable agriculture, improving maize quality and enhancing production efficiency have become critical research priorities. This paper reviews the current status and recent advances in maize quality improvement and efficiency enhancement, focusing on genetic and molecular breeding approaches, agronomic management practices, post-harvest processing technologies, and integrated strategies for sustainable production. Key quality traits discussed include nutritional composition (protein, starch, oil, and micronutrients), processing quality, and stress-related quality attributes. Efficiency enhancement pathways encompass precision agriculture, water and nutrient use efficiency, and cropping system optimization. The review also highlights the challenges and future directions, including the integration of multi-omics technologies, genome editing, and digital agriculture, to achieve simultaneous gains in quality and productivity. It is concluded that a multidisciplinary and integrated approach is essential for achieving high-quality and high-efficiency maize production to meet future global demands.

Keywords: maize (*Zea mays* L.); quality improvement; efficiency enhancement; molecular breeding; agronomic management; precision agriculture; post-harvest processing; sustainable production

 1. Introduction

Maize (*Zea mays* L.) ranks among the top three cereal crops globally, alongside rice and wheat, and contributes significantly to global food security, livestock nutrition, and industrial production (FAO, 2022). It is cultivated across diverse agro-ecological zones, from tropical to temperate regions, and serves multiple purposes including direct human consumption, animal feed, and raw material for starch, oil, ethanol, and bio-based products (Shiferaw et al., 2011). In recent decades, global maize production has increased substantially, largely driven by genetic improvement and agronomic innovation. However, the demand for maize continues to rise due to population growth, changing dietary patterns, and expanding industrial uses, particularly in developing countries (Rosegrant et al., 2009).

While yield improvement has historically been the primary breeding objective, the concept of "quality" has gained increasing attention. Maize quality is a multifaceted trait encompassing nutritional quality (e.g., protein content and quality, starch composition, oil content, vitamin and mineral levels), processing quality (e.g., milling, baking, and starch extraction properties), and safety quality (e.g., mycotoxin contamination) (Prasanna et al., 2020). Simultaneously, enhancing resource use efficiency—particularly water, nitrogen, and land—is essential for sustainable intensification, given the environmental footprint of intensive maize production (Cassman, 1999; Tilman et al., 2011).

This paper aims to provide a comprehensive review of the approaches to maize quality improvement and efficiency enhancement. It synthesizes current knowledge on genetic and molecular breeding strategies, agronomic and management practices, post-harvest technologies, and integrated systems approaches. The review also discusses emerging technologies and future perspectives, with the goal of informing research and policy directions for sustainable maize production.

 2. Genetic and Molecular Approaches to Quality Improvement

 2.1 Conventional Breeding for Quality Traits

Conventional breeding has been the cornerstone of maize quality improvement. Quality protein maize (QPM), developed through the discovery of the *opaque-2* (*o2*) mutation and subsequent modifier genes, represents a landmark achievement in improving lysine and tryptophan content (Mertz et al., 1964; Prasanna et al., 2020). QPM varieties combine high lysine and tryptophan levels with desirable agronomic and endosperm modification traits, making them nutritionally superior to normal maize. Similarly, breeding for high-oil maize has been successful, with oil content increased from approximately 4% to over 8% in some populations through recurrent selection (Lambert, 2001). Breeding for high amylose or waxy (high amylopectin) starch has also been achieved, catering to specific industrial needs (Shannon et al., 2009).

Biofortification through conventional breeding has targeted provitamin A, zinc, and iron. HarvestPlus and CIMMYT have developed provitamin A-rich maize varieties that can significantly reduce vitamin A deficiency in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America (Prasanna et al., 2020). These efforts demonstrate the power of conventional breeding combined with marker-assisted selection (MAS) to enhance nutritional quality.

 2.2 Molecular Breeding and Marker-Assisted Selection

The advent of molecular markers has accelerated quality breeding. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping has identified genomic regions controlling protein, oil, starch, and micronutrient content (Goldman et al., 1994; Zhang et al., 2008). MAS allows for the efficient introgression of favorable alleles, particularly for traits with complex inheritance and low heritability. For example, markers linked to *o2* and its modifiers have been used to develop QPM hybrids with improved agronomic performance (Babu et al., 2005). Similarly, markers for *crtRB1* and *lcyE* genes have facilitated the development of provitamin A-enriched maize (Harjes et al., 2008).

Genomic selection (GS) has emerged as a powerful tool for improving polygenic quality traits. By predicting genomic estimated breeding values (GEBVs) using genome-wide markers, GS can shorten breeding cycles and increase genetic gain for complex traits such as oil content, protein quality, and micronutrient density (Crossa et al., 2017). Integration of GS with high-throughput phenotyping and envirotyping is expected to further enhance selection accuracy and efficiency.

 2.3 Genetic Engineering and Genome Editing

Transgenic approaches have been explored to improve maize quality. For instance, genetic engineering has been used to increase lysine content by expressing deregulated lysine biosynthesis genes, to enhance provitamin A by overexpressing *crtB* and *crtI*, and to modify starch composition by altering starch synthase genes (Naqvi et al., 2009; Zhu et al., 2008). However, regulatory hurdles and public acceptance issues have limited the widespread adoption of transgenic maize for quality traits, except in a few countries.

Genome editing, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, offers precise and rapid modification of target genes without introducing foreign DNA. It has been successfully applied to knock out genes controlling amylose synthesis (*waxy*), phytic acid biosynthesis (*ZmIPK*), and lipoxygenase activity, thereby improving starch quality, mineral bioavailability, and storage stability (Liang et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2017). Genome editing holds great promise for fine-tuning quality traits while maintaining agronomic performance, although regulatory frameworks for edited crops remain under development in many countries.

 2.4 Multi-Omics and Systems Biology

Advances in genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics have provided unprecedented insights into the molecular basis of maize quality. Multi-omics integration has elucidated regulatory networks controlling kernel development, storage reserve accumulation, and nutrient partitioning (Chen et al., 2019). For example, transcriptome and metabolome analyses have revealed key genes and metabolites associated with oil and protein accumulation, offering new targets for breeding. Systems biology approaches that integrate multi-omics data with phenotypic and environmental information will be instrumental in dissecting the genetic architecture of quality traits and in designing superior varieties.

 3. Agronomic and Management Practices for Quality and Efficiency Enhancement

 3.1 Nutrient Management

Balanced nutrient management is critical for both yield and quality. Nitrogen (N) is the most limiting nutrient in maize production, and its management directly affects protein content and quality. Split application of N, use of controlled-release fertilizers, and precision N management based on soil testing and crop sensors can improve N use efficiency (NUE) and reduce environmental losses (Cassman et al., 2002). Sulfur and zinc fertilization can enhance protein quality and micronutrient density, respectively (Prasanna et al., 2020). Site-specific nutrient management (SSNM) tailored to local soil and crop conditions has proven effective in increasing yield and nutrient use efficiency across diverse environments (Dobermann et al., 2002).

 3.2 Water Management

Water scarcity is a major constraint to maize production, particularly in rainfed and semi-arid regions. Improved water management practices, such as deficit irrigation, furrow irrigation with surge flow, and the use of drought-tolerant varieties, can enhance water use efficiency (WUE) without compromising yield (Passioura, 2006). Drip irrigation and subsurface drip irrigation have been shown to improve both yield and quality by ensuring timely and uniform water supply. Additionally, mulching and conservation tillage can reduce evaporation and improve soil water retention, contributing to higher WUE.

 3.3 Cropping Systems and Crop Rotation

Cropping system optimization can enhance both productivity and quality. Maize-legume rotations, such as maize-soybean or maize-groundnut, improve soil fertility through biological nitrogen fixation and diversification of root exudates, leading to better nutrient availability and disease suppression (Snapp et al., 2010). Intercropping with legumes can also enhance protein content in maize through improved N nutrition. Conservation agriculture, which combines minimal soil disturbance, permanent soil cover, and crop diversification, has been shown to improve soil health, water infiltration, and long-term sustainability of maize-based systems (Giller et al., 2009).

 3.4 Precision Agriculture and Digital Technologies

Precision agriculture technologies, including GPS-guided machinery, remote sensing, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and variable rate application (VRA), enable site-specific management of inputs. These technologies can optimize planting density, fertilizer application, irrigation, and pest control, thereby improving both yield and quality while reducing input costs and environmental impact (Zhang et al., 2002). Proximal and remote sensing can assess crop nitrogen status, canopy cover, and yield potential in real time, facilitating timely interventions. Digital platforms and decision support systems that integrate weather, soil, and crop data are increasingly used to guide management decisions for high-quality and efficient maize production.

 3.5 Integrated Pest and Disease Management

Pests and diseases can significantly reduce both yield and quality. Integrated pest management (IPM) combines cultural, biological, and chemical control methods to minimize crop losses while reducing pesticide use. Host plant resistance, crop rotation, and biological control agents are key components of IPM in maize. For example, the use of *Bacillus thuringiensis* (Bt) maize has effectively controlled stem borers and reduced mycotoxin contamination in some regions (Wu, 2006). However, the evolution of resistance and concerns about biodiversity require careful management and monitoring.

 4. Post-Harvest Processing and Quality Preservation

 4.1 Harvesting and Drying

Timely harvesting and proper drying are essential to maintain maize quality. Delayed harvesting can lead to increased moisture content, susceptibility to mold, and mycotoxin contamination, particularly aflatoxins and fumonisins (Hell et al., 2000). Mechanical drying with controlled temperature and airflow can rapidly reduce grain moisture to safe storage levels (≤13%), preserving nutritional and processing quality. However, excessive drying temperature can cause kernel cracking and reduce milling quality.

 4.2 Storage and Mycotoxin Management

Post-harvest storage is a critical stage for quality preservation. Poor storage conditions, including high humidity, temperature fluctuations, and pest infestation, can lead to quality deterioration and mycotoxin accumulation. Hermetic storage technologies, such as airtight bags and silos, have been shown to effectively control insect pests and reduce mycotoxin contamination without chemicals (Murdock et al., 2012). Integrated mycotoxin management strategies, including resistant varieties, biological control (e.g., atoxigenic *Aspergillus flavus* strains), and good agricultural practices, are essential for ensuring food safety (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2016).

 4.3 Milling and Processing Technologies

Maize processing quality is influenced by kernel hardness, starch composition, and protein content. Dry milling, wet milling, and nixtamalization are common processes that affect the nutritional and functional properties of maize products. Advances in processing technologies, such as extrusion cooking, enzymatic modification, and fermentation, can enhance the nutritional value, digestibility, and sensory quality of maize-based foods (Rooney and Serna-Saldivar, 2015). For example, nixtamalization improves calcium availability and reduces mycotoxin levels, while fermentation can increase protein digestibility and vitamin content.

 5. Integrated Strategies for Sustainable Quality and Efficiency Enhancement

Achieving simultaneous gains in quality and efficiency requires integrated approaches that combine genetic improvement, agronomic management, and post-harvest technologies. Sustainable intensification (SI) is a framework that aims to increase productivity and quality while reducing environmental impact and enhancing resilience (Pretty et al., 2018). Key components of SI in maize systems include:

- Improved germplasm with high yield potential, quality traits, and stress tolerance;
- Precision agronomy for optimized resource use;
- Conservation agriculture for soil health and biodiversity;
- Integrated pest and disease management for reduced chemical inputs;
- Post-harvest technologies for quality preservation and value addition;
- Digital agriculture for data-driven decision making.

Policy and institutional support, including extension services, market incentives, and quality standards, are also critical for scaling up integrated strategies. Public-private partnerships and farmer participatory approaches can facilitate the adoption of improved technologies and practices.

 6. Challenges and Future Perspectives

Despite significant progress, several challenges remain. Climate change poses increasing threats to maize production through drought, heat, and pest outbreaks, which can negatively affect both yield and quality. The genetic complexity of quality traits and their interaction with the environment complicates breeding efforts. Additionally, the adoption of advanced technologies, such as genome editing and precision agriculture, is constrained by regulatory, economic, and social factors, particularly in developing countries.

Future research should focus on:

- Integrating multi-omics and systems biology to dissect quality trait architecture and identify novel breeding targets;
- Harnessing genome editing and synthetic biology for precise quality improvement;
- Developing climate-resilient, nutrient-dense maize varieties through combined conventional and molecular approaches;
- Advancing precision agriculture and digital tools for site-specific, sustainable management;
- Enhancing post-harvest value chains to reduce losses and improve food safety;
- Strengthening policy and institutional frameworks to support technology adoption and market access.

 7. Conclusion

Maize quality improvement and efficiency enhancement are essential for meeting the growing global demand for nutritious food, feed, and industrial products in a sustainable manner. This review has highlighted the diverse approaches available, ranging from genetic and molecular breeding to agronomic management and post-harvest technologies. Significant progress has been made in developing quality protein maize, biofortified varieties, and high-oil or specialty starch maize, as well as in improving resource use efficiency through precision agriculture and integrated crop management. However, achieving simultaneous gains in quality and efficiency requires integrated, multidisciplinary strategies that combine genetic innovation, agronomic optimization, and post-harvest excellence. Emerging technologies such as genome editing, multi-omics, and digital agriculture offer unprecedented opportunities, but their deployment must be accompanied by supportive policies, capacity building, and farmer engagement. By adopting integrated and sustainable approaches, it is possible to enhance maize quality and efficiency, contributing to food security, nutrition, and environmental sustainability.

 References

Babu, R., Nair, S.K., Kumar, A., Venkatesh, S., Sekhar, J.C., Singh, N.N., Srinivasan, G., and Gupta, H.S. (2005). Two-generation marker-aided backcrossing for rapid conversion of normal maize lines to quality protein maize (QPM). *Theoretical and Applied Genetics*, 111(5), 888–897.

Bandyopadhyay, R., Ortega-Beltran, A., Akande, A., Mutegi, C., Atehnkeng, J., Kaptoge, L., Senghor, A.L., Adhikari, B.N., and Cotty, P.J. (2016). Biological control of aflatoxins in Africa: current status and potential challenges in the face of climate change. *World Mycotoxin Journal*, 9(5), 771–789.

Cassman, K.G. (1999). Ecological intensification of cereal production systems: yield potential, soil quality, and precision agriculture. *Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences*, 96(11), 5952–5959.

title: 大豆设施栽培关键技术
text:
Key Technologies for Protected Cultivation of Soybean: A Review

Abstract: Protected cultivation (facility cultivation) of soybean offers a viable strategy to extend the growing season, mitigate adverse environmental conditions, and enhance yield stability. This paper reviews the key technologies involved in soybean protected cultivation, including cultivar selection, environmental regulation, sowing and planting density management, water and fertilizer regulation, pollination and pod-setting enhancement, and pest and disease control. The integration of these technologies is essential for achieving high yield and quality in facility-based soybean production. Future research should focus on precision management and intelligent control systems to further optimize protected soybean cultivation.

Keywords: soybean; protected cultivation; facility agriculture; key technologies; environmental regulation

 1 Introduction

Soybean (*Glycine max* L. Merr.) is one of the most important grain and oil crops worldwide, serving as a critical source of plant protein and edible oil for human consumption and livestock feed (Liu et al., 2020). With increasing demand for soybean products and the challenges posed by climate variability, traditional open-field cultivation alone can hardly meet production requirements. Protected cultivation, which involves growing crops under controlled or semi-controlled environmental conditions such as greenhouses, plastic tunnels, and screen houses, provides an effective approach to overcome these limitations (Heuvelink et al., 2018).

Protected soybean cultivation enables off-season production, reduces pest and disease pressure, protects plants from extreme weather events, and allows for precise management of water and nutrients. In recent years, protected cultivation of soybean has gained increasing attention, particularly for vegetable-type soybean (edamame) and specialty soybean production. However, systematic understanding of the key technologies specific to soybean facility cultivation remains limited. This paper aims to review and synthesize the critical technological components for successful soybean protected cultivation.

 2 Cultivar Selection

The choice of appropriate cultivars is the foundation of successful protected soybean cultivation. Unlike field cultivation, facility environments impose unique selection criteria:

2.1 Adaptability to Low Light. Greenhouse conditions often result in reduced light intensity compared to open field. Cultivars with high photosynthetic efficiency under low-light conditions and compact canopy architecture should be prioritized (Zhang et al., 2019).

2.2 Temperature Tolerance. Protected environments can experience temperature fluctuations. Cultivars with broad temperature adaptability and tolerance to both low and high temperature stress are preferred.

2.3 Growth Habit. Determinate or semi-determinate cultivars with short plant height and concentrated pod-setting are generally more suitable for facility cultivation, as they facilitate management and harvesting (Wang et al., 2021).

2.4 Maturity Group. Early to medium-maturing cultivars are typically chosen to allow multiple cropping cycles within a year and to fit the available facility production window.

2.5 Quality Traits. For edamame production, cultivars with large pod size, bright green color, high sucrose content, and good flavor are essential. For grain soybean, high protein or oil content may be the primary consideration.

 3 Environmental Regulation

Environmental control is the core advantage of protected cultivation. Key parameters requiring regulation include:

3.1 Temperature Management. Soybean germination requires a minimum temperature of 10–12°C, while optimal growth occurs at 25–30°C during the day and 18–22°C at night. In greenhouses, temperature can be regulated through ventilation, shading, heating systems, and thermal screens. During summer, excessive temperatures (>35°C) can cause flower abortion and pod shedding; therefore, cooling measures such as forced ventilation, fogging systems, and shade nets are necessary (Li et al., 2022).

3.2 Light Regulation. Soybean is a short-day plant, and photoperiod significantly affects flowering time and reproductive development. Supplementary lighting using LED systems with appropriate spectra (red and blue light) can promote photosynthesis and regulate flowering under short-day conditions. Conversely, in long-day environments, blackout curtains can be used to induce flowering in short-day cultivars (Meng et al., 2020).

3.3 Humidity Control. Relative humidity in the facility should be maintained at 60–75%. Excessive humidity promotes fungal diseases and reduces pollination efficiency, while overly low humidity can cause flower desiccation. Ventilation and dehumidification systems are important tools for humidity management.

3.4 CO₂ Enrichment. Elevated CO₂ concentration (700–1000 μmol·mol⁻¹) in greenhouses can significantly enhance photosynthetic rate and biomass accumulation in soybean. CO₂ enrichment is particularly beneficial during the vegetative growth stage under closed conditions (Hao et al., 2021).

 4 Sowing and Planting Density

4.1 Sowing Time. In protected cultivation, sowing time can be adjusted according to market demand and facility availability. For spring production in unheated plastic tunnels, sowing is typically conducted in late February to early March. For autumn-winter production in heated greenhouses, sowing may be performed in September to October.

4.2 Planting Density. Optimal planting density for protected soybean depends on cultivar architecture, facility type, and production objectives. Generally, a density of 15–25 plants per square meter is recommended for edamame production in greenhouses. Higher densities may increase total pod number per unit area but can also lead to excessive mutual shading and increased disease incidence (Chen et al., 2019). Proper row spacing (40–60 cm) and plant spacing (15–25 cm) should be arranged to ensure adequate air circulation and light penetration.

4.3 Seed Treatment. Before sowing, seeds should be treated with fungicides and inoculated with rhizobia to promote nodulation and nitrogen fixation. Seed priming can improve germination uniformity and seedling vigor under facility conditions.

 5 Water and Fertilizer Management

5.1 Irrigation. Drip irrigation combined with mulching film is the recommended irrigation method for protected soybean. This approach conserves water, reduces humidity, and minimizes weed growth. Irrigation scheduling should be based on soil moisture tension and crop water requirements at different growth stages. Critical irrigation periods include flowering and pod-filling stages.

5.2 Fertilization. Soybean has a high demand for nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, as well as micronutrients such as molybdenum and boron. While biological nitrogen fixation supplies a significant portion of nitrogen, supplementary application is often necessary. A balanced fertilization scheme should include:
- Basal fertilizer: compound fertilizer (N-P₂O₅-K₂O, 15-15-15) at 300–450 kg·ha⁻¹
- Topdressing at branching stage: urea at 75–150 kg·ha⁻¹
- Foliar spraying at flowering and pod-filling stages: 0.2% KH₂PO₄ and 0.1% boric acid solution

Fertigation through drip irrigation systems allows precise nutrient delivery and improves nutrient use efficiency (Zhao et al., 2020).

 6 Pollination and Pod-Setting Enhancement

Poor pod-setting is a common problem in protected soybean cultivation due to limited air movement, high humidity, and inadequate pollinator activity. Strategies to improve pod-setting include:

6.1 Mechanical Vibration. Gentle shaking of plants during flowering can facilitate pollen release and transfer, improving pollination efficiency.

6.2 Pollinator Introduction. Introducing bumblebees or honeybees into the greenhouse during flowering can significantly enhance pollination and pod-setting rates.

6.3 Plant Growth Regulators. Application of appropriate concentrations of growth regulators (e.g., paclobutrazol, uniconazole) can control excessive vegetative growth, promote reproductive development, and reduce flower and pod abscission.

6.4 Agronomic Practices. Maintaining optimal temperature and humidity during flowering, avoiding water stress, and ensuring adequate nutrition can all contribute to improved pod-setting.

 7 Pest and Disease Management

Protected environments can favor the proliferation of certain pests and diseases. Integrated pest management (IPM) strategies should be adopted:

7.1 Major Pests. Aphids, whiteflies, spider mites, and pod borers are common pests in protected soybean. Control measures include:
- Physical control: yellow sticky traps, insect-proof nets
- Biological control: release of natural enemies such as *Encarsia formosa* and *Phytoseiulus persimilis*
- Chemical control: selective insecticides applied according to economic thresholds

7.2 Major Diseases. Downy mildew, powdery mildew, anthracnose, and root rot are prevalent in facility conditions. Management strategies include:
- Cultural control: crop rotation, proper ventilation, removal of infected plant debris
- Resistant cultivars: selection of disease-resistant varieties
- Chemical control: appropriate fungicides applied preventively or curatively

7.3 Ecological Management. Maintaining a balanced ecosystem within the facility through companion planting, soil solarization, and biological soil amendments can reduce disease pressure and minimize chemical inputs (Xu et al., 2021).

 8 Conclusions and Perspectives

Protected cultivation of soybean represents a promising approach to enhance production efficiency, ensure year-round supply, and improve product quality. Key technologies reviewed in this paper include appropriate cultivar selection, precise environmental regulation, optimized sowing and density management, scientific water and fertilizer regulation, pollination enhancement, and integrated pest and disease management. The successful implementation of these technologies requires a systems approach that integrates agronomic, environmental, and engineering knowledge.

Future research directions should include: (1) developing soybean cultivars specifically bred for protected environments; (2) establishing precision management models based on crop growth simulation and sensor technology; (3) integrating intelligent control systems for automated environmental regulation; (4) exploring soilless cultivation and vertical farming systems for soybean production; and (5) evaluating the economic feasibility and sustainability of protected soybean cultivation under different agro-climatic conditions.

 References
